bird of paradise.care_tips: Water when top 2 inches of soil is dry. Keep consistently moist in growing season, reduce in winter. Bright indirect to direct light preferred - needs lots of light to flower. High humidity (50-60%) preferred. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Wipe large leaves monthly. Repot every 2-3 years. Distinctive bird-like flowers. Can grow quite large - provide adequate space. Mildly toxic to pets—may cause GI upset. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

white bird of paradise.description: Also known as: Giant bird of paradise. Large tropical plant with banana-like leaves and striking white and blue crane-shaped flowers. Grows to 6m outdoors; popular as dramatic indoor foliage plant.
white bird of paradise.care_tips: Water when top 5cm of soil is dry; reduce in winter. Bright indirect to direct light — more light encourages flowering. Medium humidity sufficient but appreciates higher. Large plant that needs space; repot every 2-3 years. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer. Leaves may split naturally with age. Prune dead leaves at base. Mildly toxic to pets.

bonsai.description: Miniature trees created through cultivation techniques - care varies by species, this is a general guide.
bonsai.care_tips: Water when soil surface is dry - check daily as small pots dry quickly. Avoid both over and under-watering. Adjust based on species needs - research your specific tree type. Bright indirect to direct light depending on species. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with bonsai fertilizer. Prune regularly to maintain shape. Repot every 2-3 years with bonsai soil mix. Requires patience and consistent care. Each species has specific requirements.

coleus.description: Also known as: Painted nettle. Colorful foliage plants in the Lamiaceae family with vibrant leaves in various patterns and colors, pinch flowers to maintain foliage.
coleus.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist, avoid letting dry out. Bright indirect light maintains vibrant colors; direct sun may fade colors. High humidity (50-60%) preferred. Fertilize every 2 weeks spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Pinch flower spikes to redirect energy into leaf growth and maintain the best foliage color, though flowering does not kill the plant. Pinch tips regularly to maintain bushy growth. Repot annually. Easy to propagate from cuttings. Annual in most climates. Mildly toxic to pets if ingested.

scientific_names: Cordyline fruticosa (syn. C. terminalis; Ti plant
cordyline.description: Tropical foliage plant with sword-shaped leaves in vibrant reds, pinks, purples, and greens. The Hawaiian ti plant holds deep cultural significance in Polynesian traditions.
cordyline.care_tips: Water when top 1-2 inches of soil are dry; keep evenly moist but not soggy. Bright indirect light for best color; tolerates lower light but colors fade. Medium humidity (50%+). Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer. Prune leggy stems by cutting back — new growth sprouts from below the cut. Brown leaf tips indicate low humidity or fluoride sensitivity — use filtered water. Hawaiian ti leaves are used for wrapping food and making hula skirts. Toxic to cats and dogs — causes vomiting and depression.

scientific_names: which is the world's largest individual flower
corpse flower.description: World's largest unbranched flower structure, producing a massive spathe that smells of rotting flesh when blooming. Blooms are rare, occurring every 7-10 years.
corpse flower.care_tips: Keep soil consistently moist but well-drained during active growth. Bright indirect light. Very high humidity (70-80%) required. Goes completely dormant after flowering — reduce water drastically. Requires large pot (60+ cm) for mature corm. Fertilize monthly during growing season with balanced fertilizer. Grows from a massive underground corm. Prefers acidic soil. Mildly toxic to pets—contains calcium oxalate. Remove the single leaf only once it has fully yellowed and collapsed at the end of the growth cycle.

croton.description: Also known as: Garden croton. Colorful tropical foliage plants in the Euphorbiaceae family with vibrant leaves in red, orange, yellow, and green, sensitive to changes.
croton.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist, avoid letting dry out. High humidity (60%+) preferred - use humidifier. Bright indirect to direct light essential to maintain vibrant colors. Sensitive to changes - avoid moving once established. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. May drop leaves if stressed (drafts, temperature changes, low humidity). Repot every 1-2 years. Wipe leaves monthly. Toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

croton mammy.description: Croton cultivar with twisted, spiral leaves in red, orange, yellow, and green.
croton mammy.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist, avoid letting dry out. Bright indirect to direct light essential for vibrant colors. High humidity (60%+) preferred. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Sensitive to drafts and changes. Toxic to pets. Repot every 1-2 years. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

cycads.description: Ancient palm-like plants in the Cycadaceae family, slow-growing with stiff fronds, many are endangered in the wild.
cycads.care_tips: Water when top 2-3 inches of soil is dry. Allow to dry slightly between waterings - avoid overwatering which causes root rot. Bright indirect to direct light preferred. Low to medium humidity is fine. Fertilize 2-3 times per year during growing season with palm fertilizer. Very slow-growing - repot every 3-5 years. Remove dead fronds at base. Toxic to pets if ingested. Ancient plants that have existed for millions of years. Research specific species for exact requirements. Remove yellowing or dead leaves promptly.

fatsia.description: Bold tropical foliage plant with large, deeply lobed palmately compound leaves.
fatsia.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Bright indirect light; tolerates lower light. High humidity preferred. Fertilize monthly spring through fall. Can grow large; prune to control size. Non-toxic to pets.

geogenanthus.description: Striking tropical plant with deeply textured, dark purple-black suckered leaves that shimmer in the light. A trending collector plant.
geogenanthus.care_tips: Keep soil consistently moist — sensitive to drought; leaf edges crisp quickly if too dry. Medium indirect light; avoid direct sun. High humidity (60%+) critical — brown leaf edges indicate low humidity. Well-draining, moisture-retentive mix. Fertilize monthly spring through fall at quarter strength. Slow grower. Sensitive to cold — keep above 18°C. Non-toxic to pets. Remove dead or yellowing foliage. Prune to maintain desired shape.

heliconia.description: Tropical rhizomatous plants with spectacular waxy bracts in red, orange, yellow, and pink. Related to banana and bird of paradise.
heliconia.care_tips: Water frequently — heliconias are heavy drinkers that need consistently moist soil. Bright indirect light indoors; filtered sun outdoors. Rich, acidic, well-drained soil with high organic matter. Very high humidity (70%+) essential — mist daily or use a humidifier. Fertilize every 2 weeks during growing season with balanced fertilizer. Protect from temperatures below 15°C. Remove dead or damaged leaves at the base. Excellent cut flowers that last 1-2 weeks. Non-toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

lemon cypress.description: Bright golden conifer with lemony scent, popular as indoor or patio plant, requires good air circulation.
lemon cypress.care_tips: Keep soil moist but not waterlogged. Excellent drainage essential. Allow top inch to dry slightly between waterings. Bright indirect to direct light preferred. Good air circulation essential - avoid stagnant air. Medium humidity (40-50%) preferred. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Prune to maintain shape. Repot every 2-3 years. Bright golden color with lemony scent. Popular as indoor or patio plant.

lucky bamboo.description: Also known as: Chinese water bamboo. Dracaena species often grown in water or soil, popular for feng shui, not a true bamboo.
lucky bamboo.care_tips: In water: Change water weekly, keep water level consistent. In soil: Water when top inch is dry. Bright indirect light preferred; avoid direct sun. Medium humidity is fine. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength (if in soil) or add to water monthly. Can be grown in water indefinitely or in soil. Popular for feng shui arrangements. Not a true bamboo. Toxic to pets. Repot every 2-3 years if in soil. Remove yellowing or damaged leaves promptly.

money tree.description: Tropical tree with palmate leaves, often sold with braided trunk; symbol of prosperity and good luck. Plants sold as money trees are often the closely related Pachira glabra.
money tree.care_tips: Water when top 2 inches of soil is dry. Avoid overwatering which causes root rot—very sensitive to soggy soil. Bright indirect light preferred. Medium to high humidity (50-60%) preferred. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Often sold with braided trunk—don't untie. Repot every 2-3 years. Remove yellowing leaves. Non-toxic to pets. Remove yellowing or dead leaves promptly.

nerve plant.description: Also known as: Mosaic plant. Colorful foliage plants in the Acanthaceae family with distinctive veining in various colors, will wilt dramatically when thirsty.
nerve plant.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist, never let dry. High humidity (70%+) essential - use humidifier or terrarium. Will wilt dramatically when thirsty but recovers quickly when watered. Bright indirect light preferred; direct sun burns leaves. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Pinch tips to encourage bushiness. Repot every 1-2 years. Perfect for terrariums. Distinctive veining in various colors.

norfolk island pine.description: Also known as: Star pine. Indoor conifer native to Norfolk Island, popular as holiday plant, not a true pine but resembles one, sensitive to dry air. Requires consistent moisture.
norfolk island pine.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist, avoid drying out completely. High humidity (50-60%) preferred - mist regularly in dry conditions or use humidifier. Bright indirect light preferred; some direct morning sun is fine. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Sensitive to dry air - brown needles indicate low humidity. Repot every 2-3 years. Popular as holiday plant. Not a true pine despite the name. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

oxalis shamrock plant.description: Plants in the Oxalidaceae family with clover-like leaves that fold at night, some species go dormant seasonally.
oxalis shamrock plant.care_tips: Keep soil moist during active growth. Reduce significantly or stop watering during dormancy when leaves die back - this is normal. Bright indirect to direct light preferred. Medium humidity (40-50%) is fine. Fertilize monthly during active growth with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Clover-like leaves fold at night. Some species go dormant seasonally - don't discard, it will regrow. Repot every 2-3 years. Toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

purple shamrock.description: Also known as: False shamrock. Clover-like plant with purple triangular leaves that fold at night; produces small pink or white flowers.
purple shamrock.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Bright indirect light preferred; some direct morning sun enhances purple. Medium humidity (40-50%). Goes dormant periodically—reduce watering when leaves die back. Fertilize monthly during active growth. Toxic to pets. Repot every 1-2 years. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

peperomia.description: Compact tropical foliage plants in the Piperaceae family with thick, succulent-like leaves.
peperomia.care_tips: Water when top 2 inches of soil is dry. More drought tolerant than many tropical plants due to succulent-like leaves. Bright indirect light preferred. Medium humidity (40-50%) is fine. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Compact growth habit. Repot every 2-3 years. Easy-care houseplants. Thick, succulent-like leaves store water. Non-toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

emerald ripple.description: Compact peperomia with deeply ridged, heart-shaped leaves in red, green, or silver.
emerald ripple.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Bright indirect light preferred; avoid direct sun. Medium humidity (40-50%). Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Susceptible to overwatering. Repot every 1-2 years when roots fill container. Non-toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

baby rubber plant.description: Peperomia with thick, glossy oval leaves; upright or trailing, not a true rubber plant.
baby rubber plant.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Bright indirect light preferred. Medium humidity (40-50%). Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Tolerates low light. Non-toxic to pets. Repot every 1-2 years when roots fill container. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

peperomia rosso.description: Compact peperomia with deeply ridged, dark green leaves and striking red undersides. Semi-succulent with low water needs. Excellent desk plant.
peperomia rosso.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry; semi-succulent so tolerates slight drought. Bright indirect light enhances red coloring. Average humidity is fine. Compact grower rarely needing repotting. Fertilize lightly spring through summer. Non-toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

peperomia watermelon.description: Compact peperomia with silver-striped leaves resembling watermelon rind.
peperomia watermelon.care_tips: Water when top 2 inches of soil is dry. Allow to dry between waterings. Bright indirect light maintains silver stripes. Medium humidity (40-50%) is fine. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Silver-striped leaves resembling watermelon rind. Compact growth habit. Repot every 2-3 years. Easy-care houseplant. Non-toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

pilea.description: Compact tropical foliage plants in the Urticaceae family with round or textured leaves.
pilea.care_tips: Water when top 2 inches of soil is dry. Allow to dry between waterings. Avoid overwatering. Bright indirect light preferred. Medium humidity (40-50%) is fine. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Compact growth habit. Round or textured leaves. Repot every 1-2 years. Easy to propagate from offsets or cuttings. Remove dead or yellowing leaves. Prune to maintain the desired shape.

chinese money plant.description: Also known as: UFO plant. Popular Pilea with round, coin-like leaves on upright stems.
chinese money plant.care_tips: Water when top 2 inches of soil is dry. Allow to dry between waterings. Bright indirect light preferred; rotate regularly for even growth. Medium humidity (40-50%) is fine. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Produces offsets (pups) that can be separated and repotted. Repot every 1-2 years. Round, coin-like leaves on upright stems. Popular and easy-care. Remove dead or yellowing leaves. Prune to maintain the desired shape.

friendship plant.description: Compact pilea with quilted, bronze-veined leaves; easy to propagate and share—hence the name.
friendship plant.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Bright indirect light preferred; avoid direct sun. High humidity (60%+) preferred. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Easy to propagate from cuttings. Repot every 1-2 years when roots fill container. Pinch tips to keep it bushy and remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

buddhist pine.description: Also known as: Kusamaki. Conifer-like evergreen with narrow leaves, popular for bonsai and topiary.
buddhist pine.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Bright indirect light. Tolerates lower light. Fertilize monthly spring through fall. Prune to maintain shape. Good for bonsai. Toxic to pets.

polka dot plant.description: Colorful foliage plants in the Acanthaceae family with spotted leaves in pink, red, or white, pinch to maintain bushy growth.
polka dot plant.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist, avoid letting dry out. High humidity (60%+) preferred - use humidifier or pebble tray. Bright indirect light maintains vibrant colors. Fertilize every 2 weeks spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Pinch tips regularly to encourage branching and maintain bushy growth. Pinch flowers immediately to prolong plant life. Repot annually. Annual in most climates. Easy to propagate from cuttings.

welwitschia.description: One of the most unusual plants on Earth — a living fossil from the Namib Desert. Each plant produces only two leaves in its entire lifetime, which grow continuously and split into straps. Can live over 1,000 years.
welwitschia.care_tips: Extremely drought tolerant but benefits from occasional deep watering. Full sun. Excellent drainage is critical — grows naturally in desert sand and gravel. Very slow growing. Nearly impossible to transplant due to a deep taproot. Non-toxic. Never cut the two leaves; only trim away dead, frayed leaf tips.

acacia.description: Large genus of trees and shrubs found across Africa, Australia, and the Americas. Iconic savanna trees with umbrella-shaped canopies. Australian wattles are the national floral emblem.
acacia.care_tips: Water sparingly once established — most acacias are extremely drought tolerant. Full sun essential. Highly adaptable to poor, sandy, or alkaline soils. Minimal fertilization needed — many species fix nitrogen. Prune to remove dead wood and shape. Fast-growing but many species are short-lived (20-30 years). African acacias have sharp thorns. Golden wattle is a prolific seeder and can be invasive outside Australia. Mildly toxic to pets (some species contain tannins).

ash.description: Deciduous tree with compound leaves and winged seeds (samaras). Valued for its strong, flexible wood used in tool handles, furniture, and baseball bats. Currently threatened by emerald ash borer.
ash.care_tips: Water regularly when young; established trees tolerate moderate drought. Full sun preferred. Adaptable to most well-drained soils, including alkaline. Fertilize annually in spring. Prune in late winter to remove dead wood and maintain form. Currently devastated by emerald ash borer (Agrilus planipennis) in North America and Europe — consult local authorities before planting. Seeds (keys) can be prolific and messy. Non-toxic to pets.

aspen.description: Deciduous tree famous for leaves that tremble in the slightest breeze. Brilliant golden-yellow fall color. Pando in Utah is the world's largest organism by mass.
aspen.care_tips: Water regularly — aspens prefer moist conditions and struggle in drought. Full sun essential. Moist, well-drained soil; tolerates a wide pH range. Fertilize annually in spring. Colonizes by root suckering — a single tree can produce a large clone colony. Best planted in groups. Short-lived as individuals (40-80 years) but clones persist for millennia. Stunning golden fall color. Prefers cool climates — struggles in hot, humid areas. Non-toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

bald cypress.description: Deciduous conifer with feathery foliage and distinctive "knees"; tolerates wet or swampy sites.
bald cypress.care_tips: Keep soil moist; tolerates standing water. Full sun preferred. Adapts to wet or dry sites once established. Fertilize in spring when young. Prune in late winter. Develops woody "knees" in wet soil. Golden fall color. Long-lived.

banyan tree.description: Strangler fig with a dramatic aerial root system that forms secondary trunks, allowing a single tree to cover several acres. National tree of India.
banyan tree.care_tips: Water regularly to keep soil consistently moist, especially when young. Full sun preferred for outdoor specimens. Rich, well-drained soil with high organic matter. Fertilize monthly during growing season. Aerial roots need humidity to develop—mist regularly in dry climates. Requires enormous space outdoors; can also be grown as an indoor bonsai. Mildly toxic to pets (latex sap causes irritation). Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

baobab.description: Also known as: Tree of Life. Massive African tree with a hugely swollen trunk that stores water, sparse crown, and edible fruit rich in vitamin C.
baobab.care_tips: Very drought-tolerant; water sparingly during growing season and withhold water entirely during dormancy (leaf-drop period). Full sun essential. Requires excellent drainage—sandy, well-drained soil. Do not overwater; trunk rot is the primary killer. Frost-sensitive—protect below 10°C. Can be grown as a bonsai or container specimen in temperate climates. Non-toxic to pets. Prune only to remove dead or damaged branches.

beech.description: Deciduous tree with smooth, silver-gray bark and glossy oval leaves that turn golden-bronze in autumn. Copper beech is a prized ornamental with purple foliage.
beech.care_tips: Water regularly during establishment and in dry spells; mature trees have extensive root systems. Full sun to partial shade. Well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil — does not tolerate compacted or waterlogged ground. Fertilize annually in early spring. Prune in late winter. Tolerates heavy pruning and makes excellent formal hedging (retains dry leaves through winter when clipped). Thin bark is easily damaged — protect from mechanical injury. Beechnuts are edible. Non-toxic to pets.

birch.description: Deciduous trees in the Betulaceae family with distinctive white or colored bark, prefer cool climates and moist soil.
birch.care_tips: Keep soil consistently moist, especially during hot weather. Prefer cool climates and moist, well-drained soil. Full sun to partial shade. Fertilize in early spring with tree fertilizer during establishment. Prune in late summer to avoid bleeding sap. Mulch around base to keep roots cool and moist. Distinctive white or colored bark. Research specific species for exact requirements. Deciduous; reduce or withhold watering when leaves drop in fall.

black locust.description: Also known as: False acacia, Robinia. Fast-growing deciduous tree in the Fabaceae family with pinnate leaves, paired thorns, and drooping clusters of fragrant white pea flowers in late spring that make prized honey; rot-resistant timber, a nitrogen fixer, and invasive far outside its native range.
black locust.care_tips: Water weekly in the first season; established trees are very drought tolerant. Full sun. Hardy to about -35°C and tolerates heat; grows at 5-35°C. Low humidity is fine. No fertilizer needed; it fixes nitrogen and thrives on poor soil. Any well-draining soil, including sand, gravel, and reclaimed land; dislikes waterlogging. Brittle wood breaks in storms and the roots sucker aggressively, forming thickets, so mow or remove suckers and avoid planting near paving. Banned or listed as invasive in parts of Europe, Australia, and North America; check locally. Toxic to pets; bark, leaves, and seeds c

bodhi tree.description: Also known as: Sacred Fig, Peepal Tree, Pipal. Tropical fig tree sacred in Buddhism, with distinctive heart-shaped leaves and long drip tips.
bodhi tree.care_tips: Full sun to partial shade. Water deeply when top 2 inches of soil dry; reduce in winter. Tolerates poor soil but prefers rich, well-drained loam. Warm temperatures above 15°C — not frost hardy. Can grow into a massive tree (30m+) in tropical climates; container culture limits size. Aerial roots may develop. Prune to shape in spring. Mildly toxic — latex sap can cause skin irritation.

bristlecone pine.description: The oldest known living organisms on Earth, with gnarled, wind-sculpted forms found at high elevations in the American West. Some specimens exceed 5,000 years old.
bristlecone pine.care_tips: Extremely drought-tolerant; water sparingly. Full sun essential. Requires excellent drainage—thrives in rocky, alkaline, nutrient-poor soil. Do not fertilize. Extremely slow-growing (may add only a few centimeters per year). Very cold-hardy. Difficult to cultivate outside its native high-altitude habitat. Non-toxic to pets. Prune dead, diseased or crossing branches, ideally during dormancy; keep the central leader or natural form.

camphor tree.description: Also known as: Camphor laurel. Massive, long-lived evergreen in the Lauraceae family with glossy aromatic leaves that smell of camphor when crushed; a revered street and temple tree in East Asia and the source of natural camphor, but invasive in Australia and the southern United States.
camphor tree.care_tips: Water deeply every week or two for the first two years; established trees are drought tolerant. Full sun. Best at 10-35°C; mature trees tolerate brief frost to about -8°C, young trees less. Medium humidity. Little fertilizer needed; a spring application of balanced fertilizer helps young trees. Adaptable to most well-draining soils, including sandy and slightly acidic ones. Grows 30 m tall and wide with shallow surface roots that lift pavement, so plant well away from buildings and drains. Drops leaves and berries year-round and self-seeds freely; check local invasive lists. Toxic to pets; cam

catalpa.description: Deciduous tree with enormous heart-shaped leaves, showy clusters of orchid-like white flowers, and long bean-like seed pods. Bold, tropical appearance in a hardy tree.
catalpa.care_tips: Water regularly when young; established trees are drought tolerant. Full sun for best flowering. Adaptable to most soils including clay and wet ground. Minimal fertilization needed. Prune in late winter — responds well to hard pruning. Known for large leaves, showy flowers, and dangling seed pods (up to 40cm long). Fast-growing and can look untidy — coarse branching and large leaf litter. Catalpa worms (sphinx moth caterpillars) are prized fishing bait. Non-toxic to pets.

cedar.description: Majestic evergreen conifer with spreading, tiered branches and aromatic wood. The Cedar of Lebanon is one of the most culturally significant trees in history.
cedar.care_tips: Water regularly when young; established trees are drought tolerant. Full sun essential. Well-drained soil; tolerates various soil types. Minimal fertilization needed — once annually in spring is sufficient. Prune only to remove dead or crossing branches. Slow-growing but eventually reaches massive size — give ample space (15-20m spread). Cedar of Lebanon is a symbol of strength and eternity. Deodar cedar is the most commonly planted landscape cedar. Aromatic wood naturally resists insects. Non-toxic to pets.

flowering cherry.description: Ornamental cherry with clouds of pink or white spring blossoms; iconic in Japanese gardens.
flowering cherry.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist during bloom. Full sun preferred. Well-draining soil. Fertilize after flowering. Prune after bloom to avoid disease; minimal pruning preferred. Short-lived (15–25 years). Susceptible to borers and diseases. Mildly toxic to pets—may cause GI upset.

chinese elm.description: Graceful deciduous or semi-evergreen tree with small leaves, fine branching, and attractive mottled bark that flakes to reveal orange, grey, and cream. The most popular species for bonsai.
chinese elm.care_tips: Water regularly — keep soil consistently moist but not waterlogged. Full sun to partial shade. Adapts to most soil types. Prune in late winter for shape. Highly resistant to Dutch elm disease. Excellent for bonsai — responds well to pruning and wiring. Non-toxic.

citrus trees.description: Evergreen fruit trees in the Rutaceae family with fragrant flowers and edible fruits, require warm climates or indoor protection.
citrus trees.care_tips: Deep soak regularly (weekly in growing season). Keep consistently moist but well-drained. Reduce watering in winter when growth slows. Full sun essential (6-8 hours daily). Fertilize monthly spring through fall with citrus-specific fertilizer. Prune after fruiting to maintain shape. Protect from frost - bring indoors or cover if temperatures drop below 32°F. Fragrant flowers precede fruit. Require warm climates or indoor protection in winter. Mildly toxic to pets—peel and foliage can cause GI upset. Evergreen; reduce watering in winter when growth slows.

coast redwood.description: The tallest trees on Earth, native to the foggy coastal forests of California and Oregon, with soft reddish bark and flat needles.
coast redwood.care_tips: Keep soil consistently moist; benefits greatly from fog or supplemental misting in dry climates. Full sun to partial shade. Prefers deep, acidic, well-drained soil rich in organic matter. Fertilize young trees in spring. Needs humidity—struggles in arid inland climates. Very fast-growing (up to 1 meter per year). Non-toxic to pets. Prune dead, diseased or crossing branches, ideally during dormancy; keep the central leader or natural form.

conifers.description: Cone-bearing evergreen trees and shrubs, include pines, spruces, firs, and cedars, provide year-round structure.
conifers.care_tips: Deep soak regularly (weekly during growing season). Water well before ground freezes in winter to prevent winter desiccation. Mulch around base to retain moisture and protect roots. Full sun preferred for most species. Fertilize in early spring with evergreen fertilizer. Prune in late winter/early spring. Many species are drought-tolerant once established. Provide year-round structure and privacy screening. Research specific species for exact requirements and mature size. Evergreen; reduce watering in winter when growth slows.

crabapple.description: Small flowering tree with spring blossoms and persistent ornamental fruit; many disease-resistant cultivars.
crabapple.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun essential. Well-draining soil. Fertilize in spring. Prune in late winter; thin for airflow. Choose disease-resistant cultivars (e.g. scab, fire blight). Fruit attracts birds. Edible fruit in some cultivars. Mildly toxic to pets—may cause GI upset.

crepe myrtle.description: Deciduous flowering tree prized for long-lasting summer blooms in pink, purple, red, or white, and attractive exfoliating bark.
crepe myrtle.care_tips: Water deeply once per week during first two years; established trees are drought-tolerant. Full sun required for best flowering — minimum 6 hours direct. Prune in late winter to shape; avoid 'crepe murder' (severe topping). Fertilize in early spring with balanced slow-release fertilizer. Good air circulation prevents powdery mildew. Non-toxic to pets.

dawn redwood.description: Deciduous conifer discovered in China in 1944, previously known only from fossils, with feathery foliage that turns russet-bronze in autumn.
dawn redwood.care_tips: Keep soil consistently moist, especially during the first few years. Tolerates wet and even temporarily flooded conditions. Full sun preferred. Prefers moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil but adapts to various conditions. Fertilize in spring with balanced fertilizer. Fast-growing (up to 60 cm per year). Deciduous—drops needles in fall. Very cold-hardy. Non-toxic to pets. Prune dead, diseased or crossing branches, ideally during dormancy; keep the central leader or natural form.

deciduous trees.description: Trees that lose their leaves seasonally, provide shade in summer and allow light in winter.
deciduous trees.care_tips: Deep soak regularly (weekly for first 2-3 years). Water well during establishment period. Mature trees are more drought tolerant but benefit from deep watering during dry spells. Full sun to partial shade depending on species. Fertilize in early spring with tree fertilizer. Prune in late winter/early spring when dormant. Mulch around base to retain moisture. Provide shade in summer, allow light in winter. Research specific species for exact requirements.

desert trees.description: Also known as: Mesquite. Trees adapted to arid desert conditions, extremely drought tolerant once established.
desert trees.care_tips: Minimal watering once established (monthly or less). Deep but infrequent watering during establishment (first 1-2 years). Allow to dry completely between waterings. Full sun essential. Well-draining soil critical. Fertilize sparingly if at all. Prune in late winter. Extremely drought tolerant once established. Adapted to arid desert conditions. Research specific species for exact requirements. Some are evergreen, others drought-deciduous. Research specific species for seasonal behavior.

dogwood.description: Deciduous trees and shrubs in the Cornaceae family with showy spring flowers and colorful fall foliage.
dogwood.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist, especially during flowering and fruit development. Prefer partial shade to full sun depending on climate. Well-drained, slightly acidic soil preferred. Fertilize in early spring with acid-loving plant fertilizer. Prune after flowering if needed. Mulch around base to retain moisture. Showy spring flowers and colorful fall foliage. Research specific species for exact requirements. Deciduous; reduce or withhold watering when leaves drop in fall.

dragon blood tree.description: Iconic umbrella-shaped tree endemic to Socotra Island, Yemen. Known for its distinctive mushroom-like canopy and crimson red resin (dragon's blood) used in traditional medicine and dyes for centuries.
dragon blood tree.care_tips: Extremely drought tolerant once established. Full sun. Well-draining soil essential. Very slow growing — can live 300-600+ years. Difficult to cultivate outside its native habitat. Hardy in warm, arid climates only. Non-toxic. Remove yellowing or damaged leaves promptly.

elm.description: Also known as: American Elm, White Elm, Water Elm. Iconic deciduous shade tree with a vase-shaped canopy, once the dominant street tree in North America.
elm.care_tips: Full sun for optimal growth — tolerates partial shade. Water deeply 1-2 times per week when young; established trees need water only during dry spells. Adapts to many soil types; prefers neutral pH (6.0-7.5). Choose Dutch elm disease (DED) resistant cultivars. Prune in late fall or winter when dormant. Non-toxic to pets and humans.

eucalyptus.description: Also known as: Cider gum. Fast-growing evergreen trees native to Australia with aromatic, often silvery-blue foliage and distinctive peeling bark; widely planted for timber, ornamental value, and essential oil.
eucalyptus.care_tips: Water deeply and infrequently once established; young trees need regular watering during the first 2 years. Full sun is essential. Well-drained, slightly acidic soil is ideal; intolerant of waterlogged conditions. Fast-growing — can add 2-3 meters per year in good conditions. Prune to shape in late winter or early spring. Many species are fire-adapted with flammable oils, so consider placement carefully. Coppice multi-stemmed types annually for fresh juvenile foliage. Toxic to pets — eucalyptus oil is harmful if ingested.

evergreen trees.description: Broadleaf trees that keep their foliage year-round, providing permanent structure, screening, and shade; for needle-bearing evergreens see Conifers.
evergreen trees.care_tips: Deep soak regularly (weekly during growing season). Water well before ground freezes in winter to prevent winter desiccation. Mulch around base to retain moisture and protect roots. Full sun to partial shade depending on species. Fertilize in early spring with evergreen fertilizer. Prune in late winter/early spring. Provide year-round structure and privacy screening. Research specific species for exact requirements. Evergreen; reduce watering in winter when growth slows.

scientific_names: most popular Christmas tree in Europe)
fir.description: Evergreen conifer with soft, flat needles and upright cones that disintegrate on the tree. Most popular Christmas tree genus alongside spruce.
fir.care_tips: Water regularly — firs prefer consistently moist soil. Full sun to partial shade; afternoon shade helpful in hot climates. Cool, moist, acidic soil rich in organic matter. Fertilize in early spring with acidic evergreen fertilizer. Minimal pruning needed — naturally forms a symmetrical cone. Prefers cool climates and struggles in heat and drought. Balsam fir produces aromatic resin used in Christmas wreaths. Fraser fir is the top-selling Christmas tree in the US. Non-toxic to pets.

fruit trees.description: Deciduous and evergreen trees grown for edible fruits, require proper pruning and often need cross-pollination.
fruit trees.care_tips: Deep soak regularly (weekly during growing season). Increase watering during fruit development. Mulch around base to retain moisture. Full sun essential (6-8 hours daily). Fertilize in early spring with fruit tree fertilizer. Prune in late winter/early spring to maintain shape and encourage fruiting. Many require cross-pollination - plant compatible varieties nearby. Thin fruit for larger, healthier fruits. Protect from late frosts during flowering. Leaves, pits and seeds of apples and stone fruits are mildly toxic to pets. Reduce watering when dormant in winter.

giant sequoia.description: Also known as: Wellingtonia. The largest trees on Earth by volume, native to the western Sierra Nevada with massive trunks and spongy, fire-resistant bark.
giant sequoia.care_tips: Water regularly during establishment (first 3-5 years); mature trees are moderately drought-tolerant. Full sun preferred. Well-drained, deep soil. Fertilize young trees in spring with balanced fertilizer. Very long-lived—some specimens exceed 3,000 years. Extremely cold-hardy. Needs space for massive trunk and root system. Non-toxic to pets. Minimal pruning needed; remove dead or damaged branches only.

ginkgo.description: Also known as: Maidenhair tree. Ancient deciduous trees in the Ginkgoaceae family, living fossil, popular street tree in China, male and female trees.
ginkgo.care_tips: Deep soak regularly during establishment. Mature trees are drought tolerant. Well-drained soil preferred. Full sun preferred. Fertilize in early spring during establishment. Prune in late winter. Ancient living fossil. Popular street tree in China. Plant male cultivars to avoid smelly fruit. Beautiful golden fall foliage. Very long-lived. Deciduous; reduce or withhold watering when leaves drop in fall. Mildly toxic to pets—may cause GI upset.

hawthorn.description: Also known as: May tree, Thornapple, Quickthorn. Small thorny trees in the Rosaceae family with white or pink spring blossom and red autumn haws loved by birds; used as specimen trees, hedging, and in Chinese medicine (shanzha).
hawthorn.care_tips: Water deeply every week or two for the first two years; established trees need water only in prolonged drought. Full sun for best flowering and fruit. Very hardy, to about -35°C; needs winter chill. Medium humidity. Fertilize sparingly; a spring top-dressing of compost is enough. Tolerates clay, chalk, and poor soils as long as drainage is reasonable. Watch for fire blight, rust, and leaf spot; choose resistant species such as C. phaenopyrum and C. crus-galli. Thorns are long, so site away from paths. Non-toxic to pets; the haws are edible. Prune in late winter to shape and remove crossing or

hornbeam.description: Hardy deciduous tree with fluted bark; excellent for hedging and topiary.
hornbeam.care_tips: Keep soil moist when young. Full sun to partial shade. Tolerates heavy pruning. Fertilize in spring when establishing. Prune in late summer; excellent for formal hedges. Fall color yellow to orange. Its dense wood earns it the name "ironwood".

horse chestnut.description: Also known as: Conker tree, Buckeye. Large deciduous trees in the Sapindaceae family with palmate leaves, showy white or red flower candles in late spring, and spiny husks holding glossy brown conkers; not the edible sweet chestnut (Castanea).
horse chestnut.care_tips: Water deeply every week or two for the first few years and in summer drought; mature trees are moderately drought tolerant but scorch in hot, dry wind. Full sun to light shade. Very hardy, to about -35°C; grows best at 5-30°C with cool, moist summers. Medium humidity. Fertilize young trees in spring; mature trees need none. Deep, moist, well-draining soil. Leaf miner, leaf blotch, and bleeding canker disfigure it in many regions, so rake up fallen leaves. Needs a lot of room: 25-35 m tall and wide, with heavy litter of flowers, leaves, and nuts. Toxic to pets; conkers, leaves, and bark contain

italian cypress.description: Also known as: Pencil pine. Iconic narrow, columnar evergreen conifer with dark green, scale-like foliage; a defining element of Mediterranean and Tuscan landscapes.
italian cypress.care_tips: Water deeply but infrequently; drought-tolerant once established — overwatering is the main killer. Full sun is essential for its tight, columnar form. Well-drained, even rocky or gravelly soil is ideal; tolerates alkaline conditions and poor soil. Minimal pruning needed — trim only to remove dead branches. Does not tolerate heavy, waterlogged clay. Protect from sustained freezing winds in marginal zones. Plant in groups for a dramatic landscape statement. Non-toxic to pets.

jacaranda.description: Deciduous to semi-evergreen tropical tree famous for spectacular violet-blue flower clusters that blanket the canopy in spring. Iconic street tree worldwide.
jacaranda.care_tips: Water regularly when young; established trees are moderately drought tolerant. Full sun essential for best flowering. Well-drained soil; tolerates sandy and slightly alkaline conditions. Fertilize once in spring with balanced fertilizer. Prune only to shape — heavy pruning reduces flowering. Best flowering occurs after a dry winter period. Fast-growing (up to 1.5m per year when young). Weak wood is susceptible to wind damage. Non-toxic to pets.

japanese maple.description: Graceful maple with delicate lobed leaves; red, green, or variegated; stunning fall color.
japanese maple.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist; avoid drought stress. Partial shade preferred—full sun can scorch leaves. Well-draining, slightly acidic soil. Fertilize lightly in spring. Prune in winter when dormant. Protect from wind. Red cultivars need some sun for color.

joshua tree.description: Iconic tree-like yucca of the Mojave Desert with twisted branches and spiky leaf clusters, a symbol of the American Southwest.
joshua tree.care_tips: Extremely drought-tolerant; water deeply but infrequently (every 2-3 weeks in summer, rarely in winter). Full sun essential—needs intense direct sunlight. Requires excellent drainage; sandy or gravelly soil ideal. Do not fertilize. Very slow-growing. Protect from frost below -10°C. Mildly toxic (saponins) to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

kapok tree.description: Massive tropical tree that can reach 60-70 meters with buttress roots and a wide canopy. Produces large pods containing silky, cotton-like fiber (kapok) used for stuffing and insulation.
kapok tree.care_tips: Water regularly when young; drought tolerant once established. Full sun. Rich, well-draining soil. Fast growing in tropical climates. Cannot tolerate frost. Sacred tree in many cultures — the Mayan World Tree. Non-toxic. Prune only to remove dead or damaged branches.

larch.description: Unique deciduous conifer that sheds its needles in autumn after turning brilliant golden-yellow. Fresh green spring foliage is remarkably soft. Native to cold, mountainous regions.
larch.care_tips: Water regularly — larches prefer moist, cool conditions. Full sun essential; does not tolerate shade. Acidic, well-drained, moist soil. Fertilize in early spring with acidic fertilizer. Minimal pruning needed. The only common conifer that drops all its needles — golden fall color rivals any deciduous tree. Prefers cool, humid mountain climates — struggles in heat and drought. Tamarack tolerates boggy conditions. Fast-growing for a conifer. Non-toxic to pets.

linden.description: Also known as: Basswood, Tilia. Deciduous shade tree with heart-shaped leaves and intensely fragrant cream-colored flowers in summer. Major urban and park tree throughout Europe.
linden.care_tips: Water regularly during establishment; moderately drought tolerant once mature. Full sun to partial shade. Prefers moist, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil. Fertilize annually in spring. Prune in late winter to maintain shape. Fragrant flowers attract bees prolifically — a major honey tree. Linden flower tea (tilleul) is a popular European herbal tea. Susceptible to aphids that produce honeydew — can make a sticky mess. Non-toxic to pets.

magnolia.description: Deciduous and evergreen trees in the Magnoliaceae family with large, fragrant flowers, many species are ancient flowering plants.
magnolia.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist, especially during flowering. Prefer consistently moist but well-drained soil. Full sun to partial shade. Fertilize in early spring with balanced fertilizer. Prune after flowering if needed. Mulch around base to retain moisture. Large, fragrant flowers. Many species are ancient flowering plants. Research specific species for exact requirements. Deciduous; reduce or withhold watering when leaves drop in fall.

star magnolia.description: Compact deciduous magnolia with fragrant star-shaped white flowers appearing before leaves in early spring; ideal small garden tree.
star magnolia.care_tips: Water regularly during first 2-3 years; established trees are moderately drought-tolerant. Full sun to partial shade; protect from late frosts that damage early blooms. Prefers moist, acidic, well-draining soil rich in organic matter. Mulch around base to retain moisture and keep roots cool. Minimal pruning needed—prune only after flowering if necessary. Fertilize in spring with acid-loving plant food. Non-toxic to pets.

mangrove.description: Tropical coastal trees adapted to saltwater environments with distinctive aerial prop roots. Vital to coastal ecosystems, providing habitat and shoreline protection.
mangrove.care_tips: Keep roots permanently submerged or in very wet soil. Full sun preferred. High humidity essential. Use brackish or saltwater for established plants; freshwater for seedlings. Fertilize sparingly — mangroves thrive in nutrient-poor conditions. Indoor cultivation possible in large containers with standing water. Prune to control size. Non-toxic to pets.

maple.description: Deciduous trees in the Sapindaceae family known for brilliant fall foliage, many species are popular landscape trees.
maple.care_tips: Deep soak regularly during establishment (first 2-3 years). Keep consistently moist but well-drained. Mature trees are more drought tolerant. Full sun to partial shade depending on species. Fertilize in early spring with tree fertilizer during establishment. Prune in late winter when dormant. Mulch around base. Brilliant fall foliage. Research specific species for exact requirements.

monkey puzzle tree.description: Also known as: Chilean Pine, Chile Pine. Ancient evergreen conifer with distinctive spiny, overlapping leaves and a striking symmetrical silhouette.
monkey puzzle tree.care_tips: Full sun to light shade. Water regularly to keep soil moist — does not tolerate drought well. Prefers cool, maritime climates with abundant rainfall. Well-drained but moisture-retentive soil. Tolerates cold to -20°C once established. Slow-growing — avoid pruning as branches do not regrow. Protect from hot, dry summer conditions. Non-toxic to pets.

moringa.description: Fast-growing, drought-tolerant tree with edible leaves, pods, seeds, and flowers. Extremely nutritious — leaves contain high levels of vitamins and minerals.
moringa.care_tips: Water deeply once established, then allow soil to dry somewhat between waterings. Full sun essential. Well-draining sandy or loamy soil. Extremely fast growing — can reach 3+ meters in the first year. Cannot tolerate frost. Prune regularly to encourage bushier growth. Non-toxic — all parts are edible.

neem tree.description: Evergreen tree native to the Indian subcontinent, widely cultivated for its medicinal and insecticidal properties. Nearly every part of the tree has been used in traditional medicine.
neem tree.care_tips: Water regularly when young; very drought tolerant once established. Full sun. Adapts to poor soils but prefers well-draining conditions. Fast growing. Cannot tolerate frost or prolonged cold. Neem oil from seeds is a popular organic pesticide. Mildly toxic if ingested in large quantities. Prune dead, diseased, or crossing branches. Best done during dormancy. Maintain central leader or natural form.

oak.description: Majestic deciduous and evergreen trees in the Fagaceae family, provide shade and wildlife habitat, many species are long-lived.
oak.care_tips: Deep soak regularly during establishment (first 2-3 years). Mature trees are drought tolerant but benefit from deep watering during extended dry periods. Full sun preferred. Fertilize in early spring with tree fertilizer during first 5 years. Prune in late winter when dormant. Mulch around base to retain moisture. Provide shade in summer. Many species live for centuries. Research specific species for exact requirements. Toxic to pets.

pine.description: Evergreen conifers in the Pinaceae family with needle-like leaves and woody cones, many species are long-lived and widely planted for timber, shelter, and ornament.
pine.care_tips: Water deeply during establishment (first 2-3 years). Mature trees are drought tolerant once established. Full sun essential - at least 6 hours daily. Prefer acidic, well-drained soil. Fertilize young trees in early spring with acid-forming fertilizer. Prune candles in spring to control growth - avoid cutting into old wood. Mulch with pine needles to maintain soil acidity. Avoid planting in waterlogged soil. Evergreen - no seasonal leaf drop. Many species live for centuries. Mildly toxic to pets—may cause GI upset.

plum blossom.description: Also known as: Chinese plum, Japanese apricot, Mei, Ume. Small deciduous tree in the Rosaceae family that flowers on bare branches in late winter with fragrant white, pink, or red blossoms; celebrated in East Asian art, and its sour fruit is pickled as umeboshi and made into plum wine.
plum blossom.care_tips: Water deeply weekly in the first two years and during dry summers; avoid waterlogging. Full sun. Hardy to about -20°C; buds open during mild spells in late winter and are rarely damaged by frost. Medium humidity. Fertilize in early spring with a balanced fertilizer; too much nitrogen reduces flowers. Well-draining, moderately fertile soil. Fruit sets best with a second cultivar nearby. Prone to the same pests and diseases as other stone fruit, so keep the canopy open. Mildly toxic to pets; leaves, stems, and pits contain cyanogenic compounds. Prune right after flowering, shortening long shoots

plumeria.description: Also known as: Frangipani. Tropical tree famous for its intensely fragrant, waxy flowers in white, yellow, pink, or red; widely associated with Hawaiian leis.
plumeria.care_tips: Water regularly during growing season but allow soil to dry between waterings; reduce to almost none in winter dormancy. Full sun essential—at least 6 hours daily for flowering. Well-draining soil critical; prone to root rot in wet conditions. Fertilize with high-phosphorus fertilizer every 2 weeks spring through fall to promote blooms. Goes dormant and drops leaves in winter—this is normal. Protect from frost. Propagates easily from cuttings—allow cut end to dry for a week before planting. Milky sap can irritate skin; mildly toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

poplar.description: Also known as: Cottonwood. Fast-growing deciduous trees valued for shade, windbreaks, and timber. Lombardy poplar is one of the most recognizable columnar trees.
poplar.care_tips: Water regularly — poplars are thirsty trees that prefer moist conditions. Full sun essential. Tolerates most soil types including wet ground. Minimal fertilization needed. Prune in late winter. Extremely fast-growing (2-3m per year). Aggressive root systems — plant at least 15m from buildings, pipes, and foundations. Female cottonwoods produce messy cotton-like seeds. Lombardy poplar is short-lived (15-25 years) and prone to canker. Non-toxic to pets.

redbud.description: Small tree with magenta flowers on bare branches in early spring; heart-shaped leaves.
redbud.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist when young. Full sun to partial shade. Well-draining soil. Fertilize in spring. Prune after flowering if needed. Nitrogen-fixing. Susceptible to canker—avoid wounding. Edible flowers. Fall color yellow.

chinese redbud.description: Large shrub or small tree with pink flowers on branches before leaves; more heat-tolerant than Eastern redbud.
chinese redbud.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist when young. Full sun to partial shade. Well-draining soil. Fertilize in spring. Prune after flowering. Tolerates heat better than C. canadensis. Often multi-trunked. Fall color yellow.

river birch.description: Multi-trunk birch with distinctive peeling cinnamon-brown bark; tolerates wet soils.
river birch.care_tips: Keep soil consistently moist; tolerates wet sites. Full sun to partial shade. Acidic soil preferred. Fertilize in spring when young. Prune in late summer to avoid sap bleed. Resistant to bronze birch borer. Heat-tolerant. Often grown multi-trunked.

royal poinciana.description: Also known as: Flamboyant, Flame tree, Gulmohar. Spreading tropical tree in the Fabaceae family with a flat umbrella crown of fern-like leaves that is smothered in scarlet-orange flowers for weeks in early summer; one of the most spectacular flowering trees in the world and a classic street tree of the tropics.
royal poinciana.care_tips: Water deeply every week or two while establishing; mature trees are drought tolerant and flower best after a dry season. Full sun. Needs frost-free conditions at 15-38°C; leaves drop in cool or dry weather and the tree dies below about -2°C. Medium humidity. Fertilize young trees two or three times a year with a balanced fertilizer; mature trees rarely need feeding. Any well-draining soil; tolerates salt and poor soil. Shallow, wide roots lift pavement and the canopy spreads 10-15 m, so plant at least 6 m from buildings and paths. Flowers after 5-10 years from seed; the long woody pods persist

serviceberry.description: Also known as: Juneberry. Small tree or large shrub with white spring flowers, edible berries, and brilliant fall color.
serviceberry.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist when young. Full sun to partial shade. Adapts to various soils. Fertilize in spring. Prune in late winter. Edible berries attract birds. Excellent fall color. Native to North America. Multi-season interest.

silk tree.description: Also known as: Mimosa tree, Persian silk tree. Fast-growing, umbrella-shaped deciduous tree in the Fabaceae family with fern-like leaves that fold at night and fluffy pink powder-puff flowers in summer; invasive in parts of the southeastern United States.
silk tree.care_tips: Water weekly during the first season; established trees are drought tolerant. Full sun. Hardy to about -18°C once established; best at 15-35°C. Low to medium humidity. Needs little fertilizer; it fixes its own nitrogen. Tolerates poor, dry, and alkaline soils; needs good drainage. Short-lived and prone to mimosa wilt (Fusarium); the seed pods and seedlings are messy and it self-sows aggressively, so check local invasive lists before planting. Toxic to pets; the seed pods contain a neurotoxic alkaloid that can cause seizures in dogs. Prune in late winter to remove dead wood and crossing limbs;

smoke tree.description: Shrub or small tree with fluffy gray-pink "smoke" plumes and purple or green foliage.
smoke tree.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun for best color and flowering. Well-draining soil. Fertilize in spring. Prune in late winter—cut hard for large leaves, light prune for plumes. Purple cultivars need full sun. Drought tolerant. Fall color orange to red. Mildly toxic to pets—sap may cause irritation; ingestion may cause GI upset.

spruce.description: Evergreen conifer with stiff, sharp needles attached individually to branches. Classic Christmas tree shape. Important timber and paper pulp trees in northern forests.
spruce.care_tips: Water regularly when young; established trees need supplemental water only during drought. Full sun preferred; tolerates light shade. Acidic, well-drained, moist soil. Fertilize in early spring with acidic evergreen fertilizer. Prune only dead or damaged branches — do not cut into old wood as it won't regrow. Shallow root system — susceptible to wind throw. Blue spruce is one of the most popular landscape conifers. Prone to spider mites in hot, dry conditions. Non-toxic to pets.

sweetgum.description: Tall deciduous tree with star-shaped leaves and spiky seed balls; brilliant fall color.
sweetgum.care_tips: Keep soil moist when young. Full sun preferred. Tolerates wet or dry soil. Fertilize in spring when establishing. Prune in late winter. Fall color red, orange, yellow. Seed balls can be messy—consider fruitless cultivars. Deep taproot.

sycamore.description: Massive deciduous tree with distinctive mottled bark that peels in patches to reveal cream, green, and tan colors. The most widely planted urban street tree worldwide.
sycamore.care_tips: Water regularly during establishment; very tolerant of drought and urban conditions once mature. Full sun preferred. Highly adaptable to most soil types and pH levels. Fertilize annually in spring. Prune in winter to maintain clearance and shape. London plane is the premier urban tree — tolerates pollution, compacted soil, heat, and heavy pruning. Distinctive bark is ornamental year-round. Produces spiky seed balls. Very large tree (30m+) — needs ample space. Non-toxic to pets.

tulip tree.description: The tallest eastern North American hardwood, with unique four-lobed leaves and tulip-shaped yellow-green flowers in late spring.
tulip tree.care_tips: Water deeply and regularly during establishment and dry spells; somewhat drought-sensitive. Full sun preferred. Prefers deep, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil. Fertilize young trees in early spring. Fast-growing shade tree. Prune in late winter when dormant. Aphids on leaves may produce sticky honeydew. Brilliant golden-yellow fall color. Non-toxic to pets.

weeping willow.description: Iconic deciduous tree with gracefully cascading branches that sweep to the ground. Fast-growing; often planted near water features and ponds for dramatic silhouette.
weeping willow.care_tips: Thrives in moist to wet soil; ideal near ponds, streams, and low-lying areas. Full sun preferred. Extremely fast-growing — can add 2-3m per year. Plant well away from foundations, septic systems, and underground pipes as roots are aggressive. Prune dead or damaged branches in late winter. Short-lived for a tree (30-50 years). Very cold-hardy. Non-toxic to pets.

willows.description: Fast-growing, water-loving trees and shrubs with flexible branches and early-spring catkins, ranging from towering white willows to shrubby pussy and dappled willows.
willows.care_tips: Keep soil consistently moist; willows thrive near water and tolerate wet sites. Full sun. Plant large species away from pipes and foundations—roots are aggressive. Prune in late winter; shrubby types can be coppiced hard every few years for fresh colored stems. Cut pussy willow catkins in late winter for arrangements. Fast growth and weak wood—susceptible to storm damage. Non-toxic to pets.

windmill palm.description: Also known as: Chinese windmill palm. The most cold-hardy palm in the world, tolerating temperatures down to -15°C. Fan-shaped leaves on a trunk covered in dark, hairy fiber.
windmill palm.care_tips: Water regularly during growing season; reduce in winter but do not let soil completely dry. Full sun to partial shade — can tolerate quite deep shade. Adaptable to most well-drained soils. Fertilize 2-3 times during growing season with palm fertilizer. Remove old, yellowing fronds at the base. Extremely cold-hardy for a palm — survives temperatures down to -15°C with mature specimens. Grows slowly (15-30cm per year). Excellent for adding tropical look to temperate gardens. Non-toxic to pets. Only remove completely brown fronds. Never cut green or yellowing fronds as the plant reclaims nutrient

wollemi pine.description: Living fossil discovered in 1994 in a remote canyon in Australia. Thought to have been extinct for 2 million years. Distinctive bubbly, chocolate-brown bark.
wollemi pine.care_tips: Water regularly; prefers consistently moist but not waterlogged soil. Partial shade to full sun. Prefers acidic, well-draining soil. Surprisingly adaptable in cultivation. Hardy to about -5°C. Slow growing. Non-toxic. Conservation status: critically endangered in the wild. Prune dead, diseased, or crossing branches. Best done during dormancy. Maintain central leader or natural form.

abelia.description: Also known as: Glossy abelia. Compact shrub with glossy leaves and tubular white-pink flowers; long bloom season.
abelia.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun to partial shade. Well-draining soil. Fertilize in spring. Prune lightly after flowering. Semi-evergreen to evergreen. Attracts pollinators. Deer resistant.

arborvitae.description: Also known as: Eastern White Cedar, Northern White Cedar. Dense, evergreen conifer widely used for hedges, privacy screens, and windbreaks.
arborvitae.care_tips: Full sun to partial shade — at least 6 hours of sun for dense foliage. Water deeply once per week when young; established trees tolerate moderate drought. Well-drained soil essential — does not tolerate waterlogged conditions. Tolerates wide pH (6.0-8.0). Prune lightly in spring to shape. Protect from heavy snow and ice damage. Contains thujone — mildly toxic if large quantities are ingested.

azaleas.description: Flowering shrubs in the Ericaceae family, part of the Rhododendron genus, prefer acidic soil and partial shade.
azaleas.care_tips: Keep soil consistently moist but well-drained (2-3 times per week). Acidic soil essential (pH 4.5-6.0) - use acidifying fertilizer and mulch with pine needles or oak leaves. Partial shade preferred - morning sun with afternoon shade is ideal. Fertilize in early spring with acid-loving plant fertilizer. Prune immediately after flowering. Mulch to keep roots cool and retain moisture. Don't plant too deep - keep root ball slightly above soil level. Research evergreen vs deciduous varieties for your climate. Deciduous varieties: reduce watering when dormant in winter. Toxic to pets.

barberry.description: Thorny shrub with red, gold, or green foliage; small berries; invasive in many regions.
barberry.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun for best color. Tolerates poor soil. Fertilize in spring. Prune in late winter—wear gloves for thorns. Deer resistant. Invasive in eastern North America—check local restrictions. Consider sterile cultivars. Mildly toxic to pets—may cause GI upset if ingested.

beautyberry.description: Deciduous shrub with arching branches and vivid magenta-purple berry clusters that encircle the stems in autumn, providing striking fall and winter interest.
beautyberry.care_tips: Water regularly during establishment; moderately drought-tolerant once mature. Full sun to partial shade—more sun means more berries. Adaptable to most well-drained soils. Fertilize lightly in spring. Can be cut back hard to the ground in late winter to rejuvenate (blooms on new wood). Berries attract birds. Non-toxic to pets.

bottlebrush.description: Australian native shrub or small tree with distinctive cylindrical flower spikes resembling bottle brushes. Flowers are typically brilliant red, attracting birds and bees.
bottlebrush.care_tips: Water regularly during establishment; very drought tolerant once mature. Full sun essential for best flowering. Highly adaptable to poor, sandy, or clay soils; tolerates some salinity. Minimal fertilization needed — native plant adapted to nutrient-poor Australian soils. Prune lightly after flowering to maintain shape — do not cut into old wood. Excellent for coastal gardens. Seed capsules persist on branches for years. Attracts hummingbirds, bees, and honeyeaters. Non-toxic to pets.

boxwood.description: Evergreen shrubs in the Buxaceae family with dense foliage, popular for hedges and topiary, slow-growing and long-lived.
boxwood.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist, especially during establishment. Well-drained soil essential. Full sun to partial shade. Fertilize in early spring with balanced fertilizer. Prune in late spring or early summer to maintain shape. Mulch around base. Dense foliage perfect for hedges and topiary. Slow-growing and long-lived. Watch for boxwood blight and pests. Evergreen; reduce watering in winter when growth slows. Toxic to pets.

burning bush.description: Shrub with corky winged branches; brilliant scarlet fall color; invasive in many areas.
burning bush.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun for best fall color. Adapts to most soils. Fertilize in spring. Prune in late winter. Invasive in eastern North America—avoid or use sterile cultivars. Berries toxic. Corky "wings" on stems distinctive. Toxic to pets.

butterfly bush.description: Also known as: Summer lilac. Arching shrub with fragrant flower spikes; attracts butterflies; can be invasive.
butterfly bush.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun essential. Well-draining soil. Fertilize in spring. Prune hard in late winter—flowers on new growth. Deadhead to prolong bloom. Invasive in some regions—choose sterile cultivars. Deer resistant.

camellia.description: Evergreen shrubs in the Theaceae family with beautiful flowers, includes tea plant, popular in Chinese gardens.
camellia.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist (weekly deep watering). Well-drained, acidic soil essential. Partial shade preferred - avoid hot afternoon sun. Fertilize in spring with acid-loving plant fertilizer. Prune after flowering. Beautiful flowers in winter/spring. Tea plant (C. sinensis) leaves are used for tea. Popular in Chinese gardens. Protect from harsh winds. Evergreen; reduce watering in winter when growth slows.

caryopteris.description: Also known as: Bluebeard. Compact shrub with blue flower clusters in late summer; silvery-gray foliage.
caryopteris.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun preferred. Well-draining soil. Fertilize in spring. Cut back hard in late winter—flowers on new growth. Drought tolerant. Attracts bees and butterflies. Deer resistant. Late-season bloomer.

cold hardy evergreens.description: Evergreen plants that tolerate cold winter temperatures, provide year-round structure and color in landscapes.
cold hardy evergreens.care_tips: Deep soak regularly during growing season. Water well before ground freezes in winter to prevent winter desiccation (brown needles). Mulch around base to retain moisture and protect roots. Full sun to partial shade depending on species. Fertilize in early spring with evergreen fertilizer. Prune in late winter/early spring. Tolerate cold winter temperatures. Provide year-round structure and color. Research specific species for exact requirements. Toxic to pets.

cotoneaster.description: Spreading shrub with herringbone branches, small leaves, and red berries; groundcover or upright.
cotoneaster.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun to partial shade. Well-draining soil. Fertilize in spring. Prune after berries drop. Fire blight susceptible. Berries attract birds. Some species invasive—check locally. Drought tolerant once established. Toxic to pets.

daphne.description: Compact, fragrant-flowering shrub prized for intensely sweet-scented winter and spring blooms. Among the most powerfully fragrant garden plants.
daphne.care_tips: Water moderately — keep evenly moist but never waterlogged; daphnes are very sensitive to root rot. Partial shade preferred; protect from hot afternoon sun. Well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil rich in organic matter. Fertilize lightly once in spring. Do not transplant or disturb roots — plant in its permanent position. Minimal pruning — does not respond well to hard cutting. Short-lived (10-15 years) but worth it for the fragrance. All parts are highly toxic, especially the berries — toxic to pets and humans.

euonymus.description: Versatile genus of evergreen and deciduous shrubs used extensively in landscaping for hedging, groundcover, and specimen planting. Includes the fiery-red burning bush.
euonymus.care_tips: Water regularly during establishment; drought tolerant once mature. Full sun to partial shade — evergreen varieties tolerate shade well. Highly adaptable to most soils. Fertilize once in spring. Prune freely to maintain shape — tolerates hard pruning. E. alatus (burning bush) has spectacular scarlet fall color but is invasive in eastern North America — banned in some states. E. fortunei 'Emerald Gaiety' is the most popular variegated groundcover. Susceptible to scale insects. All parts toxic, especially fruits — toxic to pets.

evergreen shrubs.description: Woody shrubs that retain foliage year-round, provide structure and privacy in landscapes.
evergreen shrubs.care_tips: Deep soak regularly (weekly during growing season). Keep consistently moist during establishment (first 1-2 years). Water well before ground freezes in winter to prevent desiccation. Full sun to partial shade depending on species. Fertilize in early spring with shrub fertilizer. Prune in late winter/early spring to maintain shape. Mulch around base. Provide structure and privacy year-round. Research specific species for exact requirements. Evergreen; reduce watering in winter when growth slows. Toxic to pets.

flowering quince.description: Also known as: Japonica. Thorny deciduous shrub in the Rosaceae family that covers its bare branches with red, orange, pink, or white blossoms in late winter; small fragrant fruits make jelly.
flowering quince.care_tips: Water weekly while establishing; mature shrubs are drought tolerant. Full sun for the most flowers; tolerates partial shade. Very hardy, to about -30°C; needs winter chill to bloom well. Medium humidity. Fertilize lightly in early spring. Adaptable to most well-draining soils; leaves yellow (chlorosis) in very alkaline soil. Flowers on old wood, so prune right after flowering, thinning crowded and crossing stems. Branches can be cut in late winter and forced indoors. Non-toxic to pets; the hard fruit is edible only when cooked. Remove suckers and dead wood annually.

flowering shrubs.description: Woody shrubs grown primarily for their flowers, many require specific soil pH for optimal bloom color.
flowering shrubs.care_tips: Deep soak at base regularly (weekly during growing season). Keep consistently moist during flowering period. Mulch around base to retain moisture. Full sun to partial shade depending on species. Fertilize in early spring with flowering shrub fertilizer. Many require specific soil pH for optimal bloom color (e.g., hydrangeas - acidic for blue, alkaline for pink). Prune after flowering or in late winter depending on species. Research specific species for exact requirements. Deciduous in most climates; reduce watering when dormant in winter. Toxic to pets.

forsythia.description: One of the earliest spring-blooming shrubs, covered in bright yellow flowers before leaves emerge. Fast-growing and hardy; often used as hedging or specimen plants.
forsythia.care_tips: Water regularly during first year; established plants are drought-tolerant. Full sun produces best flowering; tolerates partial shade. Prune immediately after flowering since blooms form on previous year's wood. Rejuvenate overgrown plants by cutting one-third of oldest stems to ground annually. Fertilize in early spring. Extremely cold-hardy. Non-toxic to pets.

scientific_names: 'Darkness'; Erica carnea (Winter heath) is the winter-flowering cousin
heather.description: Also known as: Scotch heather, Ling. Low evergreen shrub in the Ericaceae family forming mounds of tiny scale-like leaves, covered in late summer and autumn with spikes of pink, purple, or white bell flowers; foliage of many cultivars turns gold or red in winter.
heather.care_tips: Water regularly in the first year and in dry spells; established plants are moderately drought tolerant but hate drying out completely. Full sun for the best flowers and foliage color. Hardy to about -25°C; dislikes hot, humid summers. Medium humidity. Feed sparingly with an ericaceous (acid) fertilizer in spring. Requires acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-draining, low-nutrient soil; add peat substitute or pine bark, as it fails in lime. Mulch with pine needles. Non-toxic to pets. Shear the spent flower spikes off in early spring, cutting just below the old flowers but never into bare wood.

holly.description: Evergreen or deciduous shrub with spiny leaves and red berries; needs male and female for fruit.
holly.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist. Full sun to partial shade. Slightly acidic soil preferred. Fertilize in spring. Prune in late winter. Male and female plants needed for berries. Berries toxic. Deer resistant. Many cultivars for size and form. Toxic to pets.

hydrangeas.description: Also known as: Mophead, Lacecap. Popular flowering shrubs in the Hydrangeaceae family, flower color depends on soil pH for some varieties.
hydrangeas.care_tips: Keep soil consistently moist (2-3 times per week). Water deeply during flowering period. Mulch to retain moisture. Partial shade preferred - morning sun with afternoon shade is ideal. Fertilize in early spring with balanced fertilizer. Bigleaf hydrangeas: acidic soil (pH 5.5) produces blue flowers; alkaline soil (pH 6.5+) produces pink flowers. Prune after flowering or in late winter depending on species. Research specific type for pruning requirements - some bloom on old wood, others on new wood. Deciduous varieties: reduce watering when dormant in winter. Toxic to pets.

juniper.description: Evergreen coniferous shrubs and trees in the Cupressaceae family, drought-tolerant and versatile for landscapes.
juniper.care_tips: Water deeply but infrequently once established (every 2-3 weeks). Very drought tolerant. Well-drained soil essential. Full sun preferred. Fertilize sparingly in spring with evergreen fertilizer. Prune in late winter or early spring. Many varieties available from groundcovers to trees. Very versatile for landscapes. Evergreen; reduce watering in winter when growth slows. Mildly toxic to pets—may cause GI upset.

knock out rose.description: Disease-resistant, continuously blooming landscape rose that revolutionized home rose growing. Requires minimal maintenance compared to traditional hybrid tea roses.
knock out rose.care_tips: Water deeply once or twice a week. Full sun (6+ hours). Well-draining, slightly acidic soil. Prune in early spring to 12-18 inches. Self-cleaning — no deadheading needed. Highly resistant to black spot. Fertilize in spring and summer. Non-toxic to pets.

lavender.description: Also known as: English lavender. Aromatic flowering herbs in the Lamiaceae family with silvery foliage and fragrant purple flowers, drought-tolerant once established.
lavender.care_tips: Water when soil is dry (every 1-2 weeks once established). Well-draining soil essential - avoid heavy clay. Avoid overwatering which causes root rot. Full sun essential (6-8 hours daily). Drought-tolerant once established. Fertilize sparingly in spring with low-nitrogen fertilizer. Prune after flowering to maintain shape. Harvest flowers when buds are just opening. Silvery foliage and fragrant purple flowers. Excellent for dry gardens. Evergreen; reduce watering in winter when growth slows. Mildly toxic to pets—may cause GI upset.

leadplant.description: Native prairie shrub with silvery-gray foliage and purple flower spikes; nitrogen-fixing, drought tolerant, attracts pollinators.
leadplant.care_tips: Water when top 2 inches dry; very drought-tolerant once established. Full sun. Deep taproot fixes nitrogen—improves surrounding soil. Sandy to loamy, well-draining soil. Rarely needs fertilizer. Cut back in late winter. Slow to establish but extremely long-lived.

lilac.description: Deciduous shrubs in the Oleaceae family with fragrant spring flowers in shades of purple, pink, white, and blue.
lilac.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist during growing season. Well-drained, slightly alkaline soil preferred. Full sun essential for best flowering. Fertilize in early spring with balanced fertilizer. Prune immediately after flowering to remove spent blooms and shape. Remove old canes to rejuvenate. Fragrant spring flowers. Very cold hardy. Deciduous varieties: reduce watering when dormant in winter.

limelight hydrangea.description: Panicle hydrangea with large, cone-shaped flower clusters that emerge lime-green, turn white, then fade to pink in fall. Blooms on new wood, so reliable even after harsh winters.
limelight hydrangea.care_tips: Water regularly — prefers consistently moist soil. Partial sun to full sun. Unlike bigleaf hydrangeas, flower color is not affected by soil pH. Prune in late winter or early spring. Blooms on new wood. Very cold hardy. Toxic if ingested. Toxic to pets.

loropetalum.description: Also known as: Chinese fringe flower. Shrub with purple or green foliage and fringed white or pink flowers; related to witch hazel.
loropetalum.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun for best color. Well-draining, slightly acidic soil. Fertilize in spring. Prune after flowering. Purple cultivars need sun for color. Cold-sensitive in marginal zones. Fast-growing. Versatile size.

scientific_names: Mahonia aquifolium (syn. Berberis aquifolium; Oregon grape)
mahonia.description: Also known as: Oregon grape, Grape holly. Evergreen shrubs in the Berberidaceae family with holly-like leaflets, fragrant yellow flower clusters in winter or early spring, and blue-black berries; botanists now place them in Berberis, but gardens and nurseries keep the name Mahonia.
mahonia.care_tips: Water weekly in the first year and during summer drought; established plants are drought tolerant. Partial shade is ideal; tolerates deep shade and, with enough moisture, full sun. Hardy to about -20°C (M. aquifolium) or -12°C (M. × media); grows at 5-30°C. Medium humidity. Fertilize once in spring with a balanced fertilizer and mulch with compost. Adaptable to most well-draining soils; leaves scorch in winter wind and sun. Flowers feed early bees; tart berries make jelly. Spreads slowly by suckers. Mildly toxic to pets; roots and bark contain berberine, while ripe berries are safe in small am

mock orange.description: Also known as: Sweet mock orange, English dogwood. Deciduous shrub in the Hydrangeaceae family grown for its masses of white, intensely orange-blossom-scented flowers in late spring and early summer.
