mock orange.care_tips: Water deeply once a week during the first two years and in drought; established shrubs are fairly drought tolerant. Full sun for the heaviest bloom; tolerates partial shade. Hardy to about -30°C; grows well at 10-30°C. Medium humidity. Fertilize once in early spring with a balanced slow-release fertilizer. Adaptable to most well-draining soils. Flowers on last year's wood, so prune only right after flowering, removing a third of the oldest stems at the base to renew. Non-toxic to pets. Shorten any leggy shoots after bloom; avoid shearing, which removes next year's flowers.

mountain laurel.description: Evergreen shrub native to eastern North America with leathery leaves and stunning clusters of geometric cup-shaped flowers with unique spring-loaded stamens.
mountain laurel.care_tips: Keep soil consistently moist but well-drained; never allow to sit in standing water. Partial shade preferred—tolerates deep shade but flowers best with morning sun. Requires acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.5); mulch with pine needles or oak leaves. Fertilize lightly in spring with acid-loving plant fertilizer. Minimal pruning—remove spent flower clusters to encourage next year's bloom. Toxic to pets and humans (grayanotoxins).

nandina.description: Bamboo-like shrub with ferny foliage; red fall color and berries; invasive in Southeast US.
nandina.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun to partial shade. Adapts to most soils. Fertilize in spring. Prune to remove old canes. Toxic to pets. Berries toxic to birds—choose fruitless cultivars. Invasive in warm climates. Not a true bamboo.

ninebark.description: Hardy shrub with peeling bark and colorful foliage; white or pink flower clusters.
ninebark.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun for best color. Tolerates various soils. Fertilize in spring. Prune in late winter—rejuvenation prune if overgrown. Bark peels in layers. Purple and gold cultivars available. Native. Deer resistant. Mildly toxic to pets—bark may cause GI upset if ingested.

oleander.description: Evergreen shrub with clusters of fragrant, funnel-shaped flowers in white, pink, red, or yellow. Extremely heat- and drought-tolerant. One of the most toxic ornamental plants — all parts are poisonous.
oleander.care_tips: Water sparingly once established — extremely drought tolerant. Full sun essential for best flowering. Highly adaptable to poor, alkaline, or salty soils. Fertilize once in spring. Prune after main flowering flush to shape and remove old wood. Fast-growing and excellent as screen, hedge, or highway median planting. All parts of the plant are highly toxic — ingestion of even small amounts can be fatal to humans and animals. Do not burn trimmings (smoke is toxic). Wear gloves when pruning. Toxic to pets — extremely dangerous.

osmanthus.description: Also known as: Sweet osmanthus. Evergreen shrubs in the Oleaceae family with highly fragrant flowers, popular in Chinese gardens and tea.
osmanthus.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist (weekly deep watering). Well-drained, slightly acidic soil preferred. Full sun to partial shade. Fertilize in early spring with acid-loving plant fertilizer. Prune after flowering to maintain shape. Highly fragrant flowers in fall. Popular in Chinese gardens and tea. Can be grown in containers. Evergreen foliage. Evergreen; reduce watering in winter when growth slows.

photinia.description: Also known as: Red Robin. Evergreen shrub beloved for its brilliant red new growth that matures to glossy dark green. One of the most popular hedging plants in Europe.
photinia.care_tips: Water regularly during establishment; moderately drought tolerant once mature. Full sun for best red color on new growth; tolerates partial shade but produces less vivid color. Well-drained soil preferred. Fertilize in spring with balanced fertilizer to encourage new red growth. Prune 2-3 times per year for hedges — each pruning stimulates a flush of red new leaves. Susceptible to leaf spot (Entomosporium) in humid climates — ensure good air circulation. Fast-growing. Mildly toxic to pets (contains cyanogenic glycosides in seeds).

pieris.description: Also known as: Lily of the valley shrub, Andromeda. Evergreen shrub with cascading clusters of bell-shaped white or pink flowers in spring and colorful new growth in shades of red, bronze, or pink.
pieris.care_tips: Keep soil consistently moist but not waterlogged; water deeply during dry periods. Partial shade preferred—morning sun with afternoon shade is ideal. Requires acidic soil (pH 4.5-6.0); amend with peat or sulfur if needed. Mulch with pine needles or bark to maintain acidity. Prune lightly after flowering to shape. Fertilize in spring with acid-loving plant food. All parts toxic to pets and humans (grayanotoxins).

plumbago.description: Also known as: Cape leadwort. Sprawling subtropical shrub with clusters of sky-blue phlox-like flowers blooming profusely from spring through fall. Excellent for fences, arbors, and containers.
plumbago.care_tips: Water regularly during bloom season; drought-tolerant once established. Full sun produces heaviest flowering; tolerates partial shade. Prune hard in late winter to encourage bushy growth. Fertilize monthly during growing season. Fast grower; can become leggy without pruning. Mildly toxic — may cause skin irritation. Protect from hard frost.

privet.description: Dense, fast-growing shrub widely used for formal hedging. Semi-evergreen to evergreen depending on climate. Tolerates heavy pruning and shaping, making it the classic hedge plant.
privet.care_tips: Water regularly during establishment; moderately drought tolerant once mature. Full sun to partial shade. Highly adaptable to most soil types and pH levels. Fertilize once in spring. Prune 2-3 times per year for formal hedges — responds vigorously to hard pruning. Extremely fast-growing (30-60cm per year). Some species (L. lucidum, L. sinense) are highly invasive in many regions — check local regulations before planting. Small white flowers have a strong scent (unpleasant to some). Berries and leaves are mildly toxic to pets.

firethorn.description: Also known as: Pyracantha. Thorny evergreen shrub with masses of small white spring flowers followed by spectacular clusters of orange, red, or yellow berries in autumn and winter.
firethorn.care_tips: Water regularly during establishment; drought tolerant once mature. Full sun for best berry production; tolerates partial shade. Adaptable to most well-drained soils. Fertilize once in spring. Prune after flowering to shape and control growth — wear thick gloves (very sharp thorns). Excellent wall shrub or informal hedge with built-in security (thorns deter intruders). Berries persist through winter, providing vital food for birds. Can be trained as espalier on walls and fences. Berries are mildly toxic raw but can be cooked into jelly. Mildly toxic to pets.

rhododendrons.description: Evergreen and deciduous flowering shrubs in the Ericaceae family, prefer acidic soil and partial shade, many are large-growing.
rhododendrons.care_tips: Keep soil consistently moist but well-drained (2-3 times per week). Acidic soil essential (pH 4.5-6.0) - use acidifying fertilizer and mulch with pine needles or oak leaves. Partial shade preferred - morning sun with afternoon shade is ideal. Protect from hot afternoon sun. Fertilize in early spring with acid-loving plant fertilizer. Prune immediately after flowering if needed. Mulch to keep roots cool and retain moisture. Don't plant too deep. Research specific variety for mature size - some grow very large. Deciduous varieties: reduce watering when dormant in winter. Toxic to pets.

rose of sharon.description: Upright shrub with late-summer hibiscus flowers; can self-seed prolifically.
rose of sharon.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun preferred. Well-draining soil. Fertilize in spring. Prune in late winter. Choose sterile cultivars to avoid seed spread. Flowers on new growth. Drought tolerant. Single or double flowers.

roses.description: Classic flowering shrubs in the Rosaceae family with fragrant blooms, require good air circulation.
roses.care_tips: Regular deep watering at base (2-3 times per week during growing season). Avoid wetting leaves to prevent disease (black spot, powdery mildew). Mulch around base to retain moisture. Full sun essential (6-8 hours daily). Fertilize monthly spring through fall with rose fertilizer. Prune in late winter/early spring. Deadhead spent flowers to encourage reblooming. Good air circulation essential to prevent disease. Research specific type for exact requirements. Deciduous in most climates; reduce watering when dormant in winter.

scientific_names: Salvia yangii (syn. Perovskia atriplicifolia; Russian sage)
russian sage.description: Upright perennial with lavender-blue flower spikes and silvery foliage; aromatic.
russian sage.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun essential. Well-draining soil; drought tolerant. Fertilize sparingly. Cut back to ground in late winter. Deer resistant. Attracts pollinators.

spirea.description: Versatile shrub with spring or summer flowers; mound-forming or cascading forms.
spirea.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun preferred. Adapts to most soils. Fertilize in spring. Spring bloomers: prune after flowering. Summer bloomers: prune in late winter. Tough and easy. Many cultivars for size and color.

tree peony.description: Woody shrub peony producing enormous, ruffled flowers (15-25cm across) in spring. Called the 'King of Flowers' in Chinese culture with over 1,500 years of cultivation.
tree peony.care_tips: Water regularly but do not overwater — root rot is the main killer. Morning sun with afternoon shade is ideal; protect blooms from hot afternoon sun. Rich, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil. Fertilize after flowering with balanced fertilizer and again in early fall. Do NOT cut back woody stems in winter (unlike herbaceous peonies). Plant the graft union 10-15cm below soil surface. Very slow-growing but extremely long-lived. Flowers are among the largest and most spectacular in the plant kingdom. Non-toxic to pets.

viburnum.description: Deciduous and evergreen shrubs in the Adoxaceae family with showy flowers, colorful berries, and fall foliage.
viburnum.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist, especially during flowering and fruiting. Well-drained soil preferred. Full sun to partial shade. Fertilize in early spring with balanced fertilizer. Prune after flowering if needed. Mulch around base. Showy flowers, colorful berries, and fall foliage. Many species attract birds. Research specific species for exact requirements. Deciduous varieties: reduce watering when dormant in winter.

weigela.description: Architectural shrub with trumpet flowers in spring; green, gold, or variegated foliage.
weigela.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun for best bloom. Well-draining soil. Fertilize in spring. Prune after flowering—remove old wood. May rebloom lightly. Hummingbird magnet. Deer resistant. Many cultivars for size and leaf color.

wintersweet.description: Also known as: Japanese allspice, Làmei. Deciduous shrub in the Calycanthaceae family whose waxy, translucent yellow flowers open on bare stems in the depths of winter and release a powerful sweet fragrance; a treasured winter garden plant in China.
wintersweet.care_tips: Water weekly while establishing and in summer drought; mature shrubs are fairly drought tolerant. Full sun or light shade; a warm wall sheltered from winter wind shows the flowers best. Hardy to about -15°C; flowers open on mild winter days from December to February. Medium humidity. Fertilize once in spring with a balanced fertilizer and mulch with compost. Fertile, well-draining soil; tolerates chalk. Slow to start, as seedlings take 5-7 years to bloom, so buy a grafted or cutting-grown plant. Cut stems for indoor fragrance in winter. Toxic to pets; the seeds contain the alkaloid calycanthin

witch hazel.description: Deciduous shrub or small tree that blooms in late winter to early spring with fragrant, spidery, ribbon-like flowers in yellow, orange, or red when most other plants are dormant.
witch hazel.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist, especially during establishment. Partial shade to full sun; afternoon shade beneficial in hot climates. Prefers moist, acidic, well-drained soil rich in organic matter. Fertilize lightly in spring. Minimal pruning needed—prune right after flowering if shaping is desired. Valued for winter interest when little else blooms. Non-toxic to pets.

yew.description: Ancient evergreen conifer with dark green needles and red berry-like arils. Extremely long-lived and tolerant of heavy pruning; one of the finest hedge and topiary plants.
yew.care_tips: Water regularly when young; established yews tolerate drought. Partial sun to full shade — one of few conifers thriving in deep shade. Well-drained soil essential — yews will not tolerate wet feet. Prune anytime for shaping; responds well to hard renovation pruning. Fertilize in early spring. Extremely cold-hardy. All parts highly toxic to pets and humans except the red aril flesh.

agapanthus.description: Also known as: African lily. Clump-forming perennial with strap-shaped leaves and spectacular rounded clusters of blue, purple, or white trumpet flowers on tall stalks.
agapanthus.care_tips: Water regularly during growing season; reduce in winter. Full sun produces best flowering. Performs best when slightly root-bound — do not over-pot. Divide congested clumps every 4-5 years after flowering. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with high-potassium fertilizer. Evergreen types less cold-hardy than deciduous. Mulch in cold climates. Mildly toxic if ingested. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

agastache.description: Also known as: Hyssop. Aromatic perennial with dense spikes of tubular flowers in orange, pink, purple, or blue; a magnet for hummingbirds, bees, and butterflies.
agastache.care_tips: Water sparingly once established; very drought-tolerant and sensitive to overwatering, especially in winter. Full sun (6+ hours) is essential for the most flowers and most aromatic foliage. Excellent drainage is critical — thrives in lean, sandy, or gravelly soil and struggles in heavy clay. Do not cut back in fall; leave stems standing through winter for protection, then prune to new growth in spring. Short-lived (3-5 years) but self-seeds freely. Deer and rabbit resistant due to aromatic foliage. Non-toxic to pets — anise hyssop leaves are even edible for humans.

alstroemeria.description: Also known as: Peruvian lily, Lily of the Incas. Tuberous perennials in the Alstroemeriaceae family with azalea-like, speckled flowers in every color but blue on 30-100 cm stems from early summer to frost; one of the longest-lasting cut flowers.
alstroemeria.care_tips: Water deeply once a week during growth, more in heat; the fleshy roots rot in waterlogged soil but need moisture to keep flowering. Full sun, with afternoon shade where summers are hot. Prefers 10-27°C; hardy to about -10°C with a deep winter mulch, so perennial in zones 7-10. Medium humidity. Feed every 2-3 weeks with a high-potash liquid fertilizer while in flower. Fertile, well-draining soil; plant tubers 15-20 cm deep and handle them gently, as they are brittle. Slow to establish, then spreads into a clump; can become invasive in mild climates. Non-toxic to pets, though the sap can irritat

asters.description: Fall-blooming perennial flowering plants in the Asteraceae family, provide late-season color with daisy-like flowers.
asters.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist (2-3 times per week). Water deeply during flowering period. Full sun preferred for best flowering. Fertilize in early spring with balanced fertilizer. Pinch back in early summer to encourage bushier growth and more flowers. Divide every 2-3 years in spring. Stake tall varieties. Remove spent flowers to encourage more blooms. Excellent for fall color. Attract butterflies and pollinators. Research perennial vs annual varieties. Herbaceous perennials die back; reduce watering when dormant.

astilbe.description: Also known as: False spirea. Feathery plumes in pink, white, or red; thrives in moist shade.
astilbe.care_tips: Keep soil consistently moist. Partial to full shade; burns in full sun. Rich, well-draining soil. Fertilize in spring. Divide every 3–4 years. Deadhead spent plumes. Attracts pollinators. Deer resistant.

bee balm.description: Also known as: Bergamot. Native perennial with shaggy red, pink, or purple flowers; aromatic foliage.
bee balm.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist. Full sun to partial shade. Well-draining soil. Fertilize in spring. Prone to mildew—plant for airflow, choose resistant cultivars. Deadhead to prolong bloom. Divide every 2–3 years. Attracts hummingbirds and bees.

black eyed susan.description: Also known as: Gloriosa daisy. Herbaceous perennials in the Asteraceae family with bright yellow daisy-like flowers and dark centers, native wildflowers.
black eyed susan.care_tips: Water deeply once per week during growing season. Drought tolerant once established. Well-drained soil preferred. Full sun essential for best flowering. Fertilize in early spring with balanced fertilizer. Deadhead spent flowers to encourage reblooming. Self-seeds readily. Divide every 3-4 years. Bright yellow daisy-like flowers. Native wildflowers. Herbaceous perennials die back; reduce watering when dormant.

blazing star.description: Prairie native with tall purple flower spikes; attracts butterflies and pollinators; drought tolerant.
blazing star.care_tips: Water when top 1-2 inches dry; drought-tolerant once established. Full sun essential for upright growth. Well-draining soil; avoid wet winter conditions. No fertilizer needed on average soil. Excellent cut flower. Key monarch butterfly nectar source in late summer. Cut back spent flower stalks after blooming. Cut to the ground in late fall.

scientific_names: Lamprocapnos spectabilis (syn. Dicentra spectabilis; Old-fashioned bleeding heart)
bleeding heart.description: Also known as: Old-fashioned bleeding heart. Graceful heart-shaped flowers on arching stems; foliage goes dormant in summer heat.
bleeding heart.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist. Partial to full shade. Rich, well-draining soil. Fertilize in spring. Foliage yellows and dies back in summer—plant with later emergers. Divide in fall. Long-lived. Toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

butterfly weed.description: Native milkweed with bright orange flowers; essential for monarch butterflies.
butterfly weed.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun essential. Well-draining, drier soil; avoid wet feet. Drought tolerant. Do not use pesticides—host plant for monarchs. Taproot—difficult to transplant. Leave seed pods for wildlife. Toxic to pets. Cut spent flower stems to encourage rebloom; cut back to the ground in late fall or early spring.

canterbury bells.description: Also known as: Bellflower, Garden campanula. Classic cottage garden biennials and perennials with bell-shaped flowers in blue, purple, pink, and white. Distinct from the alpine campanula species.
canterbury bells.care_tips: Water regularly to keep soil evenly moist but not waterlogged. Partial shade to full sun; afternoon shade in hot climates. Well-drained, neutral soil enriched with organic matter. Fertilize in spring with balanced fertilizer. Deadhead spent flowers to extend bloom season. C. medium is a biennial (flowers in second year, then dies); most others are true perennials. Stake taller varieties. Slugs can be problematic — use organic slug control. Divide perennial varieties every 3-4 years. Non-toxic to pets.

catmint.description: Mounding perennial with lavender-blue flower spikes; aromatic, cat-attracting foliage.
catmint.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun preferred. Well-draining soil. Drought tolerant. Shear after first bloom for rebloom. Deer resistant. Low maintenance. Spreads by rhizomes—divide if needed. Mildly toxic to pets—may cause GI upset. Cut back spent flower stalks to encourage reblooming. Cut to ground level in late fall or early spring.

chrysanthemums.description: Also known as: Florist's chrysanthemum. Fall-blooming perennial flowering plants in the Asteraceae family, provide late-season color, many varieties available.
chrysanthemums.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist (2-3 times per week). Water deeply during flowering period. Full sun essential (6-8 hours daily). Fertilize in early spring and again in midsummer with balanced fertilizer. Pinch back until mid-July to encourage bushiness and more flowers. Divide every 2-3 years in spring. Stake tall varieties. Excellent for fall color. Many are treated as annuals but are perennials in zones 5-9. Research hardiness for your zone. Herbaceous perennials die back; reduce watering when dormant. Mildly toxic to pets—may cause GI upset.

columbine.description: Also known as: Granny's Bonnet. Delicate woodland perennial with distinctive spurred flowers in vivid color combinations—red & yellow, blue & white, pink & purple. Blooms mid-spring to early summer; attracts hummingbirds. Short-lived (3-4 years) but self-seeds freely to naturalize.
columbine.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist. Partial shade preferred in hot climates. Well-draining soil. Fertilize in spring. Short-lived but self-seeds. Leaf miners common—remove affected leaves. Hummingbird magnet. Mildly toxic to pets—may cause GI upset. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

common milkweed.description: Essential Monarch butterfly host plant; fragrant pink flowers; spreads by rhizomes; full sun.
common milkweed.care_tips: Water when top 1-2 inches of soil is dry. Full sun preferred; drought tolerant once established. Well-draining soil. Fertilize lightly in spring if needed; many prairie natives prefer lean soil. Toxic to pets. Cut spent flower stems to encourage rebloom; cut back to the ground in late fall or early spring.

compass plant.description: Tall prairie native with large yellow flowers; leaves orient north-south; drought tolerant.
compass plant.care_tips: Water when top 2 inches dry; extremely drought-tolerant once established. Full sun. Deep taproot (15+ ft) makes transplanting difficult—site carefully. Well-draining, lean soil. No fertilizer. Basal leaves orient north-south (hence the name). Slow to bloom from seed (3-5 years). Cut back spent flower stalks to encourage reblooming. Cut to ground level in late fall or early spring.

coreopsis.description: Cheerful yellow daisies; long bloom season, low maintenance.
coreopsis.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun preferred. Well-draining soil. Drought tolerant. Deadhead for prolonged bloom. Cut back in midsummer to rejuvenate. Some cultivars sterile—no deadheading needed. Deer resistant.

creeping thyme.description: Also known as: Mother of thyme. Low mat-forming herb with tiny flowers; aromatic, walkable groundcover.
creeping thyme.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun essential. Well-draining, lean soil. Drought tolerant. Shear after flowering. Tolerates light foot traffic. Ideal between paving stones. Edible. Deer resistant. Remove yellowing or damaged leaves promptly.

culver s root.description: Native perennial with white candelabra flower spikes; attracts butterflies; prefers moist soil.
culver s root.care_tips: Water when top 1-2 inches of soil is dry. Full sun preferred; drought tolerant once established. Well-draining soil. Fertilize lightly in spring if needed; many prairie natives prefer lean soil. Mildly toxic to pets—roots are potent; keep away from pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

daisies.description: Daisy-like flowering plants in the Asteraceae family, include both annual and perennial types with white or colored petals.
daisies.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist (2-3 times per week). Water at base to avoid wetting flowers. Full sun preferred for best flowering. Fertilize monthly during growing season with balanced fertilizer. Deadhead regularly to encourage continuous blooming. Divide perennials every 2-3 years in spring or fall. Cut back after flowering. Many are excellent cut flowers. Attract butterflies and pollinators. Research specific type (annual vs perennial) for exact requirements. Herbaceous perennials die back; reduce watering when dormant. Mildly toxic to pets—may cause GI upset.

daylilies.description: Also known as: Daylily. Hardy perennial flowering plants in the Asphodelaceae family, each flower lasts one day but plants produce many blooms.
daylilies.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist (2-3 times per week). Water deeply during flowering period. Full sun to partial shade - more sun equals more flowers. Fertilize in early spring and after first bloom with balanced fertilizer. Divide every 3-5 years in spring or fall to maintain vigor. Remove spent flowers daily. Cut back foliage in fall or spring. Very low-maintenance and drought-tolerant once established. Research reblooming varieties for extended flowering. Herbaceous perennials die back; reduce watering when dormant. Toxic to pets.

deer fern.description: Evergreen hardy fern of cool, moist woodlands with dimorphic fronds: sterile fronds spread outward while narrow fertile fronds grow upright from the center. Excellent for shaded, acidic garden beds.
deer fern.care_tips: Keep soil consistently moist but not waterlogged; never let it dry out completely. Partial to full shade; direct sun scorches fronds. Plant in acidic, humus-rich soil that holds moisture. Mulch with leaf mold or bark. Fertilize lightly in spring if at all. Very cold-hardy (zones 5-8); needs no winter watering outdoors. Non-toxic to pets. Remove brown or dead fronds at the base in early spring; avoid cutting green fronds.

delphinium.description: Tall spikes of blue, purple, or white flowers; may need staking. Toxic.
delphinium.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist. Full sun preferred. Rich, well-draining soil. Fertilize in spring. Stake tall varieties. Deadhead to encourage rebloom. Short-lived—replace every 2–3 years. Protect from slugs. All parts toxic to humans and pets. Toxic to pets.

dianthus.description: Also known as: Pinks. Compact plants with fragrant, fringed flowers; pinks, carnations, and sweet william.
dianthus.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun essential. Well-draining, neutral to alkaline soil. Fertilize in spring. Deadhead for rebloom. Avoid wet foliage—crown rot. Short-lived in humid climates. Many cultivars for size and flower type. Mildly toxic to pets—may cause GI upset.

carnation.description: One of the world's oldest cultivated flowers, grown for over 2,000 years. Prized for ruffled, fragrant blooms in almost every color. A staple in the cut flower industry.
carnation.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry; avoid wetting foliage. Full sun (6+ hours). Well-draining, neutral to slightly alkaline soil. Deadhead regularly to encourage repeat blooming. Stake tall varieties. Fertilize monthly during growing season. Mildly toxic to pets.

echinacea.description: Also known as: Coneflower, Purple coneflower. Hardy native perennial with daisy-like flowers featuring a prominent spiny central cone, popular with pollinators.
echinacea.care_tips: Full sun — minimum 6-8 hours daily for best flowering. Drought-tolerant once established; water at soil level to avoid fungal disease. Well-drained, loamy soil with neutral pH (6.5-7.0). Extremely cold-hardy; thrives in zones 3-9. Deadhead to extend bloom season or leave seedheads for winter bird food. Divide clumps every 3-4 years. Non-toxic to pets.

false indigo.description: Also known as: Wild indigo. Native legume with blue flowers and blue-gray foliage; nitrogen-fixing; drought tolerant.
false indigo.care_tips: Water when top 1-2 inches of soil is dry. Full sun preferred; drought tolerant once established. Well-draining soil. Fertilize lightly in spring if needed; many prairie natives prefer lean soil. Mildly toxic to pets—may cause GI upset if ingested. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

field scabious.description: European wildflower with lavender pincushion flowers; long blooming; attracts butterflies.
field scabious.care_tips: Water when top 1-2 inches dry; moderate drought tolerance once established. Full sun to partial shade. Well-draining, alkaline-leaning soil. Light spring fertilizer. Lavender-blue pincushion flowers June-September. Deadhead for extended bloom. Beloved by butterflies and pollinators. European meadow native.

foxglove.description: Tall spikes of tubular, bell-shaped flowers in pink, purple, or white; biennial or short-lived perennial. All parts are toxic.
foxglove.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun to partial shade depending on species. Fertilize in spring. Mulch to retain moisture. Prune as needed for shape. All parts highly toxic to humans and pets. Contains cardiac glycosides. Toxic to pets.

gaillardia.description: Also known as: Blanket Flower. Colorful daisy-like perennials and annuals with red, yellow, and orange bicolor flowers. Drought tolerant and long-blooming, excellent for pollinators.
gaillardia.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun to partial shade depending on species. Fertilize in spring. Mulch to retain moisture. Prune as needed for shape. Non-toxic to pets.

gaura.description: Also known as: Bee blossom. Graceful perennial with slender, wiry stems bearing delicate white or pink flowers that dance in the breeze from late spring to frost.
gaura.care_tips: Water sparingly once established; drought-tolerant and prone to root rot in wet soils. Full sun produces the most floriferous display. Well-drained, lean soil is ideal — rich soil promotes floppy growth. Cut back by one-third after the first bloom flush to encourage reblooming. May be short-lived (3-5 years) but self-seeds readily in favorable conditions. Does not transplant well due to a deep taproot — site carefully when planting. Non-toxic to pets.

goldenrod.description: Native perennial with yellow flower plumes in fall; important for pollinators; drought tolerant.
goldenrod.care_tips: Water when top 1-2 inches dry; drought-tolerant once established. Full sun to light shade. Adapts to most soils. Minimal fertilizer; rich soil causes floppy growth. Cut back in late winter. Does NOT cause hay fever (wind-pollinated ragweed blooms simultaneously). Vital late-season pollinator plant.

great mullein.description: Tall biennial with velvety leaves and yellow flower spike; drought tolerant; self-seeds.
great mullein.care_tips: Water when top 1-2 inches of soil is dry. Full sun preferred; drought tolerant once established. Well-draining soil. Fertilize lightly in spring if needed; tolerates lean soil; European wildflower. Mildly toxic to pets—seeds and compounds may cause GI upset; keep away from pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

hardy geranium.description: Also known as: Cranesbill. True perennial geraniums with cup-shaped flowers and rounded leaves; low-maintenance groundcover for borders.
hardy geranium.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun to partial shade; afternoon shade in hot climates. Well-draining soil enriched with compost. Fertilize lightly in spring. Shear after first bloom flush for tidy rebloom. Spreading groundcover; divide every 3-4 years. Deer and rabbit resistant. Non-toxic to pets. Cut back after the first flush of blooms to encourage rebloom; trim spent foliage in fall.

hardy hibiscus.description: Also known as: Rose mallow. Cold-hardy perennial hibiscus producing dinner-plate-sized flowers (up to 30 cm) in white, pink, red, and bicolor from mid-summer to frost.
hardy hibiscus.care_tips: Water consistently to keep soil evenly moist; thrives near ponds and in rain gardens. Full sun (6+ hours) is essential for maximum flowering. Rich, moisture-retentive soil amended with compost is ideal. Fertilize monthly during the growing season with balanced fertilizer. Cut stems to 10-15 cm in late fall after frost kills the foliage — new growth emerges late in spring (don't give up on it!). Mulch the crown in cold zones for extra winter protection. Non-toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

sneezeweed.description: Also known as: Helen's flower. Late-summer to fall perennial with daisy-like flowers in warm tones of yellow, orange, red, and bicolor, featuring distinctive raised central cones.
sneezeweed.care_tips: Keep soil consistently moist during the growing season; does not tolerate prolonged drought. Full sun (6+ hours) is essential for upright growth and maximum flowering. Average to rich, moisture-retentive soil is ideal. Pinch stem tips in late spring to promote bushier, more compact growth and more flowers. Divide every 3-4 years in spring to maintain vigor and prevent center die-out. Mildly toxic if ingested — the common name refers to dried leaves historically used as snuff, not allergenic pollen.

hellebore.description: Also known as: Lenten rose. Shade-loving perennials that bloom in late winter to early spring with nodding flowers in white, pink, purple, green, or burgundy.
hellebore.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist but well-drained; reduce watering once established. Partial to full shade preferred—avoid hot afternoon sun. Rich, humus-laden soil with neutral to slightly alkaline pH. Fertilize in late winter or early spring with balanced fertilizer. Remove old foliage in late winter before flowers emerge. Self-sows readily. Toxic to pets and humans (protoanemonin). Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

herbaceous perennials.description: Non-woody perennial flowers that die back in winter and regrow from roots in spring, provide long-term garden structure.
herbaceous perennials.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist (weekly deep watering during growing season). Deep watering encourages strong root systems. Mulch around plants to retain moisture and suppress weeds. Full sun to partial shade depending on species. Fertilize in early spring with balanced fertilizer. Deadhead spent flowers to encourage reblooming. Cut back dead foliage in late fall or early spring. Divide every 3-5 years to maintain vigor. Provide long-term garden structure. Research specific species for exact requirements. Herbaceous perennials die back; reduce watering when dormant.

heuchera.description: Also known as: Coral Bells. Versatile shade-loving perennial grown primarily for its colorful foliage in shades of purple, bronze, lime, peach, and silver. Delicate bell-shaped flowers on wiry stems.
heuchera.care_tips: Water regularly to keep soil evenly moist; do not let dry out completely. Partial shade to full shade — dark-leaved varieties tolerate more sun. Mulch around crown to keep roots cool. Divide every 3-4 years when crown rises above soil. Cut back spent flower stalks. Fertilize in spring with slow-release fertilizer. Excellent for containers, borders, and woodland gardens. Non-toxic to pets.

hollyhock.description: Tall, stately biennial to short-lived perennial producing towering spikes of large, saucer-shaped flowers in a wide range of colors from summer into fall.
hollyhock.care_tips: Water at the base when the top inch of soil is dry; avoid overhead watering to reduce rust disease. Full sun and a sheltered position protected from strong winds is ideal, as stems can reach 2-3 meters tall. Well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost produces the best results. Stake tall varieties to prevent toppling. Watch for hollyhock rust — remove and destroy affected leaves promptly. Sow seeds in summer for blooms the following year. Non-toxic to pets and humans. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

hostas.description: Also known as: Funkia. Shade-loving perennial foliage plants in the Asparagaceae family, grown for their attractive leaves in various colors and sizes.
hostas.care_tips: Keep soil consistently moist (2-3 times per week). Mulch to retain moisture and keep roots cool. Partial to full shade preferred - morning sun is fine but avoid hot afternoon sun. Fertilize in early spring with balanced fertilizer. Divide every 3-5 years in spring or fall. Remove flower stalks after blooming to focus energy on foliage (unless you enjoy the flowers). Watch for slugs and snails which love hostas. Excellent for shade gardens. Herbaceous perennials die back; reduce watering when dormant. Toxic to pets. Cut back spent flower stalks; cut to ground level in late fall or early spring.

irises.description: Perennial flowering plants in the Iridaceae family with distinctive sword-like leaves and showy flowers, include bearded and beardless types.
irises.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist during growth and flowering (spring). Allow to dry slightly after flowering. Many prefer well-drained soil. Full sun essential for best flowering (6-8 hours daily). Fertilize in early spring with low-nitrogen fertilizer. Divide bearded irises every 3-4 years in late summer. Plant rhizomes with top exposed to sun. Remove spent flowers. Cut back foliage in fall. Research specific type (bearded, beardless, bulbous) for exact requirements. Herbaceous perennials die back; reduce watering when dormant. Toxic to pets.

ironweed.description: Native perennial with purple flowers; thrives in moist soils; attracts butterflies.
ironweed.care_tips: Water when top 1-2 inches of soil is dry. Full sun preferred; prefers consistently moist soil. Well-draining soil. Fertilize lightly in spring if needed; many prairie natives prefer lean soil. Mildly toxic to pets—may cause irritation. Cut back to the ground in late fall or early spring.

japanese anemone.description: Elegant fall-blooming perennials with simple pink or white flowers on tall, wiry stems, thriving in partial shade where few other plants flower in autumn.
japanese anemone.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist during growing season; more drought-tolerant once established. Partial shade preferred—tolerates morning sun but avoid hot afternoon exposure. Rich, moist, well-drained soil. Fertilize in spring with balanced fertilizer. Can spread by underground runners—may need containment. Cut back after frost kills foliage. Mildly toxic to pets (protoanemonin).

japanese painted fern.description: Hardy deciduous fern with silvery-gray fronds brushed with purple and burgundy along the midribs; one of the most colorful ferns for shaded gardens.
japanese painted fern.care_tips: Keep soil consistently moist but not soggy, especially in the first season. Partial to full shade; a little morning sun deepens the silver and purple tones, but hot afternoon sun scorches fronds. Rich, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil. Mulch to retain moisture. Fertilize lightly in spring. Fronds die back after frost; cut them to the ground in late fall or early spring. Divide crowded clumps in spring. Non-toxic to pets.

joe pye weed.description: Also known as: Sweet Joe Pye. Tall native with pink-purple flower clusters; prefers moist to wet soil; butterfly magnet.
joe pye weed.care_tips: Prefers consistently moist to wet soil — excellent for rain gardens and stream banks. Partial sun to full sun; tolerates more shade than most prairie plants. Grows 4-7 feet tall — plant at back of border. Pink-purple flower clusters in mid to late summer attract butterflies prolifically. Cut back in spring. Does not typically need staking. Fertilize lightly in spring if soil is lean. Non-toxic.

red hot poker.description: Striking architectural perennials with dense, torch-like flower spikes in fiery shades of red, orange, and yellow. Native to southern Africa.
red hot poker.care_tips: Water moderately during establishment; drought tolerant once mature. Full sun essential for best flowering. Well-drained soil critical — crown rot is the main killer, especially in wet winter soil. Fertilize once in spring with balanced fertilizer. Do not cut back foliage in winter — tie leaves in a bundle over the crown to protect from cold and wet. Remove spent flower spikes to encourage reblooming. Excellent hummingbird and pollinator magnet. Divide every 3-4 years. Non-toxic to pets.

lantana.description: Bold clusters of flowers in orange, pink, yellow, or red; attracts butterflies; heat-tolerant.
lantana.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun preferred. Fertilize in spring. Mulch to retain moisture. Prune as needed for shape. Toxic to pets. Perennial in frost-free zones (USDA 9-11); grown as annual in cooler climates.

lily of the valley.description: Fragrant white bell flowers on arching stems; spreads by rhizomes; classic shade plant.
lily of the valley.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist. Partial to full shade. Rich, well-draining soil. Fertilize in spring. Mulch to retain moisture. Divide when crowded. Highly toxic to humans and pets if ingested. Toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

lupine.description: Also known as: Garden lupine. Tall spikes of pea-like flowers in blue, purple, pink, yellow, and bicolors; nitrogen-fixing perennial that enriches soil.
lupine.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry; avoid wet winter conditions. Full sun essential. Well-draining, slightly acidic soil. Avoid fertilizer—lupines fix nitrogen. Deadhead spent spikes for possible rebloom. Taproot makes transplanting difficult. Short-lived (3-4 years) but self-seeds. Toxic to pets and humans if ingested.

maximilian sunflower.description: Prairie native with tall stems of yellow flowers; spreads by rhizomes; bird and pollinator favorite.
maximilian sunflower.care_tips: Water when top 1-2 inches dry; very drought-tolerant once established. Full sun essential. Adapts to most soils including clay. No fertilizer needed. Spreads by rhizomes—may need division every 3-4 years. Tall (6-10 ft); stake or plant with support. Important late-fall pollinator food source. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

meadow cranesbill.description: European geranium with blue-violet flowers; long blooming; low maintenance.
meadow cranesbill.care_tips: Water when top 1-2 inches dry; moderate drought tolerance once established. Full sun to partial shade. Well-draining soil; tolerates clay. Light spring fertilizer. Violet-blue saucer flowers June-August. Cut back after first flush for rebloom. Self-seeds moderately. European meadow wildflower; deer resistant.

meadow sage.description: Salvia with violet-blue flower spikes; long blooming; drought tolerant once established.
meadow sage.care_tips: Water when top 1-2 inches dry; moderate drought tolerance. Full sun for best flowering. Well-draining soil; avoid winter wet. Light spring fertilizer optional. Deadhead spent spikes to encourage reblooming through fall. Deer resistant. Aromatic foliage. Excellent hummingbird and bee plant.

mexican hat.description: Native prairie wildflower with distinctive drooping yellow or red-brown petals surrounding a tall central cone.
mexican hat.care_tips: Very drought-tolerant once established; water sparingly, every 1-2 weeks in dry spells. Full sun essential—at least 6 hours daily. Thrives in poor, well-drained soil; avoid rich or wet conditions. Do not fertilize—excess nutrients reduce flowering. Self-sows freely. Non-toxic to pets. Deadhead spent blooms to prolong flowering. Cut back in late fall.

new england aster.description: Native fall bloomer with purple daisy flowers; attracts butterflies; prefers moist soil.
new england aster.care_tips: Water regularly but tolerates drier conditions than many moisture-loving natives. Full sun required for best flowering and compact growth. Grows 3-6 feet tall; pinch stems in early summer to reduce height and increase branching. Masses of purple daisy flowers from September through frost — essential late-season pollinator plant. Cut back to ground in late fall or early spring. Well-draining soil preferred. Non-toxic.

oxeye daisy.description: European wildflower with white petals and yellow centers; naturalizes; drought tolerant.
oxeye daisy.care_tips: Water when top 1-2 inches of soil is dry. Full sun preferred; drought tolerant once established. Well-draining soil. Fertilize lightly in spring if needed; tolerates lean soil; European wildflower. Mildly toxic to pets—may cause GI upset if ingested. Deadhead spent flowers to prevent self-seeding. Cut back to the ground in fall.

painted daisy.description: Also known as: Pyrethrum. Colorful daisy-like flowers in pink, red, or white with ferny foliage; natural source of pyrethrin insecticide.
painted daisy.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun to partial shade depending on species. Fertilize in spring. Mulch to retain moisture. Prune as needed for shape. Toxic to pets—contains pyrethrins; keep away from pets.

penstemon.description: Also known as: Beardtongue. Tubular flowers on upright stems in many colors; native North American perennial, drought-tolerant, attracts hummingbirds.
penstemon.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun to partial shade depending on species. Fertilize in spring. Mulch to retain moisture. Prune as needed for shape. Non-toxic to pets.

peony.description: Herbaceous and tree perennials in the Paeoniaceae family with large, fragrant flowers in spring, long-lived garden favorites.
peony.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist during growing season. Well-drained, fertile soil preferred. Full sun to partial shade. Fertilize in early spring with balanced fertilizer. Plant with eyes (buds) 2 inches below soil surface. Support heavy blooms with stakes. Cut back foliage in fall. Long-lived - can thrive for decades. Large, fragrant flowers. Herbaceous perennials die back; reduce watering when dormant. Ants on buds are normal and harmless—they feed on bud nectar. Mildly toxic to pets—may cause GI upset.

phlox.description: Also known as: Garden phlox. Fragrant clusters of flowers in summer in many colors; cottage garden staple. Needs good air circulation to prevent mildew.
phlox.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun to partial shade depending on species. Fertilize in spring. Mulch to retain moisture. Prune as needed for shape. Non-toxic to pets. Choose mildew-resistant cultivars. Space for air circulation. Avoid overhead watering.

poppy.description: Iconic flowering plants with papery, crepe-like petals in vibrant reds, oranges, yellows, and pinks. Includes annual and perennial species. California poppy is the state flower of California.
poppy.care_tips: Water sparingly — most poppies are drought tolerant and rot in wet soil. Full sun essential. Excellent drainage critical — sandy or gravelly soil preferred. Do not fertilize heavily. Direct sow seeds in fall or early spring; most species resent transplanting. Oriental poppies go dormant after flowering (foliage dies back in summer, returns in fall). California poppies self-sow prolifically and are excellent for wildflower meadows. Deadhead to extend bloom. Mildly toxic to pets.

prairie coneflower.description: Prairie native with drooping yellow petals around a tall cone; drought tolerant.
prairie coneflower.care_tips: Water when top 1-2 inches dry; very drought-tolerant once established. Full sun. Lean, well-draining soil preferred. No fertilizer needed. Distinctive columnar seed head (like a sombrero). Self-seeds readily. Deadhead to prevent excessive spreading or leave for winter bird food.

prairie dock.description: Tall prairie native with large heart-shaped leaves and yellow flowers; deep taproot.
prairie dock.care_tips: Water when top 2 inches dry; very drought-tolerant once established via deep taproot. Full sun. Lean to average soil. No fertilizer. Large basal leaves (up to 18 inches) with tall, mostly leafless flower stalks to 8 ft. Slow to establish from seed but extremely long-lived. Cut back spent flower stalks; cut to ground level in late fall or early spring.

primrose.description: Low-growing spring-flowering perennials with rosettes of crinkled leaves and cheerful flowers in nearly every color. One of the first flowers of spring in temperate gardens.
primrose.care_tips: Keep soil consistently moist but not waterlogged — primroses wilt quickly in dry conditions. Partial shade preferred; protect from hot afternoon sun. Rich, humus-filled, moisture-retentive soil. Fertilize lightly in spring with balanced fertilizer. Deadhead spent flowers to prolong bloom. Divide clumps every 2-3 years after flowering to maintain vigor. Cool-season plants that go semi-dormant in hot summers. P. obconica can cause skin irritation (wear gloves). Mildly toxic to pets.

rattlesnake master.description: Prairie native with yucca-like leaves and spherical white flower clusters; drought tolerant.
rattlesnake master.care_tips: Water when top 1-2 inches dry; drought-tolerant once established. Full sun. Well-draining, lean soil. No fertilizer. Yucca-like spiny leaves are unusual for a prairie plant (actually in the carrot family). Excellent dried flower. Important pollinator plant; attracts diverse native bees. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

salvia.description: Also known as: Ornamental sage, Garden salvia. Herbaceous perennials and annuals in the Lamiaceae family grown for long-blooming spikes of purple, blue, red, or pink flowers; many are drought-tolerant and loved by hummingbirds. Culinary sage is listed under Herbs.
salvia.care_tips: Water deeply but infrequently once established (every 1-2 weeks). Drought tolerant. Well-drained soil essential. Full sun preferred. Fertilize sparingly in spring. Deadhead spent flowers to encourage reblooming. Cut back in late fall or early spring. Many species are drought-tolerant. Spikes of colorful flowers. Attract hummingbirds and butterflies. Herbaceous perennials die back; reduce watering when dormant. Non-toxic to pets.

scabiosa.description: Also known as: Pincushion flower. Charming perennial with delicate, domed flower heads studded with pin-like stamens in lavender, blue, pink, white, and deep burgundy; a pollinator magnet blooming from early summer to frost.
scabiosa.care_tips: Water regularly to keep soil evenly moist during establishment; once established, moderately drought tolerant. Full sun (6+ hours) is essential for prolific flowering. Well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil is ideal — struggles in heavy, acidic clay. Deadhead spent flowers consistently to encourage continuous blooming throughout the season. Good air circulation prevents crown rot, which is the main cause of death — avoid mulching directly against the crown. Divide every 3-4 years in spring to maintain vigor. Attracts butterflies and bees prolifically. Non-toxic to pets.

sedum perennials.description: Also known as: Stonecrop. Hardy succulent perennials with fleshy leaves and clusters of star-shaped flowers. Includes tall upright types and low-growing groundcovers. Extremely drought tolerant.
sedum perennials.care_tips: Water deeply but infrequently once established (every 2-3 weeks). Very drought tolerant. Well-drained soil essential. Full sun preferred. Fertilize sparingly in spring. Deadhead spent flowers or leave for winter interest. Cut back in late winter. Drought-tolerant groundcovers. Clusters of star-shaped flowers. Attract butterflies. Herbaceous perennials die back; reduce watering when dormant.

shade perennials.description: Perennial plants adapted to woodland and shade conditions, often prefer rich organic soil.
shade perennials.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist (weekly watering). Many prefer consistent moisture but well-drained soil. Avoid waterlogged conditions. Partial to full shade preferred. Rich organic soil preferred - amend with compost. Fertilize in early spring with balanced fertilizer. Mulch to retain moisture. Deadhead spent flowers. Divide every 3-5 years. Adapted to woodland conditions. Research specific species for exact requirements. Herbaceous perennials die back; reduce watering when dormant.

shasta daisy.description: Classic white daisy-like flowers with golden yellow centers; reliable, long-blooming garden perennial.
shasta daisy.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun to partial shade depending on species. Fertilize in spring. Mulch to retain moisture. Prune as needed for shape. Mildly toxic to pets—may cause GI upset or skin irritation if ingested.

smooth blue aster.description: Native aster with blue-purple flowers in fall; smooth leaves; drought tolerant.
smooth blue aster.care_tips: Water when top 1-2 inches dry; drought-tolerant once established. Full sun to light shade. Adapts to most soils including clay. Minimal fertilizer. Pinch stems in June for bushier growth and more flowers. Critical late-season nectar source for monarchs and native bees.

swamp milkweed.description: Monarch host plant with pink flowers; prefers moist to wet soil; native to wetlands.
swamp milkweed.care_tips: Water when top 1-2 inches of soil is dry. Full sun preferred; tolerates moist soil. Well-draining to moist soil. Fertilize lightly in spring if needed. Toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

sweet william.description: Biennial to short-lived perennial in the Dianthus family, producing dense, flat-topped clusters of fragrant flowers in red, pink, white, and bicolor patterns.
sweet william.care_tips: Water at the base when the top inch of soil is dry; avoid wetting foliage to prevent fungal issues. Full sun (6+ hours) produces the best blooms. Well-drained, slightly alkaline soil is ideal. Deadhead spent flowers to extend blooming and prevent self-seeding if unwanted. Sow seeds in summer for blooms the following spring. Fertilize in spring with a balanced slow-release fertilizer. Mildly toxic if ingested in large quantities.

globe thistle.description: Architectural perennial with spherical, steel-blue flower heads and spiny, silvery-gray foliage. The national flower of Scotland (Cirsium thistle). Excellent for dried flower arrangements.
globe thistle.care_tips: Water sparingly — extremely drought tolerant once established. Full sun essential. Adaptable to most well-drained soils, including poor and sandy ground. Do not fertilize — excess nutrients make plants floppy. Globe thistles (Echinops) are well-behaved garden plants; true thistles (Cirsium, Carduus) can be aggressive seeders. Excellent for pollinators — bees and butterflies are strongly attracted to the flowers. Cut flower heads before fully opening for dried arrangements. Non-toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

verbena.description: Clusters of small flowers in purple, pink, or white on wiry stems; heat-tolerant perennial that attracts butterflies.
verbena.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry; moderate drought tolerance once established. Full sun essential—at least 8 hours. Well-draining soil; avoid wet conditions. Fertilize every 2-3 weeks during bloom season. Deadhead regularly for continuous flowering spring through frost. Pinch tips for bushier growth. Attracts butterflies. Mildly toxic to pets.

speedwell.description: Also known as: Veronica. Cottage garden perennial with upright spikes of small blue, purple, pink, or white flowers. Excellent for pollinators and long-lasting in the border.
speedwell.care_tips: Water moderately — prefers evenly moist soil but tolerates some drought once established. Full sun for best flowering. Well-drained soil; does not tolerate wet winter conditions. Fertilize once in spring with balanced fertilizer. Deadhead spent spikes to encourage continuous bloom. Cut back in late fall. Divide clumps every 3-4 years. Very attractive to bees and butterflies. Low-maintenance and reliable. Non-toxic to pets.

viper s bugloss.description: European wildflower with blue coiled flower spikes; biennial or short-lived perennial; full sun.
viper s bugloss.care_tips: Water when top 1-2 inches of soil is dry. Full sun preferred; drought tolerant once established. Well-draining soil. Fertilize lightly in spring if needed; tolerates lean soil; European wildflower. Toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

wild bergamot.description: Native bee balm with lavender flowers; aromatic foliage; drought tolerant; attracts pollinators.
wild bergamot.care_tips: Water when top 1-2 inches dry; drought-tolerant once established. Full sun to partial shade. Well-draining soil; avoid wet conditions. No fertilizer needed. Aromatic leaves make excellent tea (related to bee balm). Spreads by runners—divide every 3 years. Powerhouse pollinator plant. Remove yellowing or damaged leaves promptly.

yarrow.description: Also known as: Milfoil. Hardy perennial with flat-topped flower clusters in white, yellow, pink, or red above ferny, aromatic foliage; drought-tolerant and pollinator-friendly.
yarrow.care_tips: Water when the top inch of soil is dry; once established, yarrow is very drought-tolerant and prefers lean, dry conditions. Full sun (6+ hours) is essential — shaded plants become floppy and produce fewer flowers. Well-drained, poor to average soil is ideal; rich soil causes weak stems and excessive spreading. Deadhead spent clusters to encourage reblooming. Divide clumps every 3-4 years to maintain vigor. Toxic to pets — contains thujone and other irritants.

yellow coneflower.description: Yellow-petaled Echinacea species native to the Ozarks; drought tolerant prairie wildflower.
yellow coneflower.care_tips: Water when top 1-2 inches dry; drought-tolerant once established. Full sun essential. Well-draining, lean soil. No fertilizer needed. Drooping yellow petals with prominent brown cone. Self-seeds freely. Leave seed heads for winter bird food. Long bloom period (July-September). Deadhead to prolong blooming or leave seed heads for winter interest. Cut back in spring.

african daisy.description: Also known as: Cape daisy, Osteospermum. Bushy South African daisies in the Asteraceae family with flowers in white, purple, pink, yellow, orange, and bicolors, often with a steel-blue center; they bloom heaviest in the cool of spring and autumn and close at night.
african daisy.care_tips: Water when the top 3 cm of soil is dry; established plants tolerate short dry spells but flower better with steady moisture. Full sun. Prefers 10-28°C; flowering slows in midsummer heat and resumes when nights cool. Perennial in zones 10-11 (O. jucundum to zone 8); grown as an annual elsewhere. Medium humidity. Feed every 2-3 weeks with a balanced liquid fertilizer, especially in containers. Well-draining, moderately fertile soil. Watch for aphids and downy mildew in damp weather. Non-toxic to pets. Deadhead often; shear back by a third in midsummer to refresh and trigger an autumn flush.

ageratum.description: Also known as: Floss flower. Compact bedding annual in the Asteraceae family with fluffy, powder-puff clusters of blue, lavender, pink, or white flowers from early summer to frost.
ageratum.care_tips: Water regularly to keep the soil evenly moist; dwarf types wilt quickly in heat. Full sun to light afternoon shade in hot climates. Grows best at 15-30°C and is killed by frost. Medium humidity. Fertilize monthly with a balanced fertilizer. Well-draining, moderately rich soil. Powdery mildew appears in crowded, humid plantings; space plants for air flow. Grown as an annual everywhere. Mildly toxic to pets and livestock; contains pyrrolizidine alkaloids. Deadhead or shear lightly in midsummer to keep flowers coming.

alyssum.description: Also known as: Sweet alyssum. Low mounds of tiny white, pink, or purple flowers with honey fragrance; ideal for edges and containers.
alyssum.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun preferred; tolerates light shade. Well-draining soil. Fertilize every 2-3 weeks with balanced fertilizer. Deadhead to prolong bloom. Cool-season annual—plant in early spring or fall.

angelonia.description: Also known as: Summer snapdragon. Upright spikes of snapdragon-like flowers in purple, pink, or white; heat-tolerant and low-maintenance.
angelonia.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun essential. Heat and drought tolerant once established. Fertilize every 2-3 weeks. No deadheading needed. Thrives in hot, humid summers.

bacopa.description: Trailing plant with small white, pink, or blue flowers; ideal for hanging baskets and container edges.
bacopa.care_tips: Keep soil consistently moist; avoid drying out. Full sun to partial shade. Fertilize every 2 weeks with bloom fertilizer. Pinch back to encourage bushiness. Heat-tolerant. Perfect for spillover in containers.

begonia.description: Annual and perennial flowers in the Begoniaceae family with colorful blooms and attractive foliage, shade-tolerant.
begonia.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist but not waterlogged (2-3 times per week). Well-drained soil essential. Partial shade to full shade preferred - avoid direct sun. Fertilize every 2-3 weeks with balanced fertilizer. Deadhead spent flowers. Mulch to retain moisture. Colorful blooms and attractive foliage. Shade-tolerant. Research specific type for exact requirements. Annual; grown for one season; no winter watering needed. Toxic to pets.

wax begonia.description: Compact begonia with waxy green or bronze leaves and clusters of flowers in white, pink, or red; shade-tolerant.
wax begonia.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist. Partial shade to full shade preferred; avoid hot afternoon sun. Fertilize every 2 weeks. Deadhead to encourage blooms. Toxic to pets. Ideal for shady borders and containers.

calendula.description: Also known as: Pot Marigold, English Marigold, Mary's Gold. Cool-season annual with edible, vibrant orange and yellow flowers used in cooking and herbal skincare.
calendula.care_tips: Full sun to light afternoon shade. Water regularly until established; mature plants tolerate some drought. Prefers cool weather (15-24°C) — flowers decline in summer heat. Slightly acidic to neutral soil (pH 6.0-7.0). Deadhead frequently for continuous blooming. Self-seeds prolifically if allowed. Excellent companion plant — deters aphids and attracts beneficial insects. Non-toxic to pets; flowers are edible.

calibrachoa.description: Miniature petunia-like flowers in many colors; prolific bloomer for containers and hanging baskets.
calibrachoa.care_tips: Water regularly; keep soil consistently moist. Full sun preferred. Fertilize every 2 weeks with bloom fertilizer. Self-cleaning—no deadheading needed. Deadhead or shear if leggy. Thrives in heat.

celosia.description: Also known as: Cockscomb. Bold tropical annual with flower heads in distinctive plume, crest, or brain-like comb shapes; colors include brilliant red, orange, yellow, pink, and purple.
celosia.care_tips: Water when the top inch of soil is dry; consistent moisture promotes best blooming but avoid waterlogged soil. Full sun (6+ hours) is essential for vibrant color and sturdy growth. Well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost is ideal. Fertilize every 2-3 weeks with balanced liquid fertilizer. Deadhead to encourage branching and more blooms. Heat-loving; plant after all frost danger has passed. Excellent for cutting and dried flower arrangements. Non-toxic to pets.

cleome.description: Also known as: Spider flower. Tall, dramatic annual with spidery flower clusters in pink, purple, or white atop long stems, self-sowing freely for return displays.
cleome.care_tips: Water regularly but allow soil to dry slightly between waterings; moderately drought-tolerant once established. Full sun preferred; tolerates light shade. Average, well-drained soil. Fertilize monthly with balanced fertilizer. Deadhead to extend blooming or leave some for self-sowing. Heat and humidity tolerant. Thorny stems—handle with gloves. Annual; grown for one season; no winter watering needed. Non-toxic to pets.

cool season annuals.description: Annual flowers that prefer cooler temperatures, often planted in fall or early spring for winter/spring blooms.
cool season annuals.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist (2-3 times per week). Water at base to avoid wetting flowers and leaves. Consistent moisture important during flowering period. Partial sun to full sun depending on species. Fertilize every 2 weeks with balanced fertilizer. Deadhead spent flowers to encourage continuous blooms. Mulch to retain moisture. Annual - replant each season.

cosmos.description: Also known as: Garden cosmos. Annual flowers in the Asteraceae family with delicate, daisy-like blooms in shades of pink, white, and purple, easy to grow.
cosmos.care_tips: Water regularly but allow to dry between waterings (2-3 times per week). Drought tolerant once established. Well-drained soil preferred. Full sun essential. Fertilize sparingly - too much fertilizer reduces blooms. Deadhead spent flowers to encourage continuous blooms. Self-seeds readily. Delicate, daisy-like blooms. Attract butterflies and bees. Annual; grown for one season; no winter watering needed.

annual dahlia.description: Seed-grown dahlia varieties treated as annuals, producing colorful single or semi-double flowers all summer without the need to store tubers over winter.
annual dahlia.care_tips: Water deeply 2-3 times per week; consistent moisture important during flowering. Full sun essential—at least 6 hours daily. Rich, well-drained soil. Fertilize every 2-3 weeks with balanced fertilizer during blooming. Deadhead spent flowers to encourage continuous blooms. Pinch growing tips when young for bushier plants. Frost-sensitive—plant after last frost. Mildly toxic to pets.

china pink.description: Fringed flowers in pink, red, or white with spicy fragrance; compact form for borders and containers.
china pink.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun preferred. Well-draining, slightly alkaline soil. Fertilize every 2-3 weeks. Deadhead to prolong bloom. Cool-season performer. Mildly toxic to pets—may cause GI upset.

dusty miller.description: Also known as: Silver ragwort. Silver-foliage annual (perennial in mild climates) grown for its deeply lobed, felt-textured, silvery-white leaves that provide contrast in borders and containers.
dusty miller.care_tips: Water when the top inch of soil is dry; drought-tolerant once established. Full sun intensifies the silver coloring; tolerates part shade but becomes leggier. Well-drained soil is essential — susceptible to root rot in wet conditions. Pinch off small yellow flower buds to maintain foliage form and prevent the plant from declining after bloom. Low fertilizer needs; feed once in spring. Mildly toxic if ingested.

cornflower.description: Classic blue (or pink, white) annual flowers with thistle-like blooms; bee-friendly and easy from seed.
cornflower.care_tips: Water when top 1-2 inches of soil is dry. Full sun preferred; drought tolerant once established. Well-draining soil. Fertilize lightly or not at all—prefers lean soil. Direct-sow in spring. Self-seeds. Deadhead regularly to prolong blooming; pinch tips early for bushier plants.

forget me not.description: Also known as: Woodland Forget-Me-Not, Scorpion Grass. Charming biennial with clusters of tiny sky-blue flowers and a heart-shaped petal arrangement.
forget me not.care_tips: Partial shade to dappled light — tolerates morning sun with afternoon shade. Keep soil consistently moist but not soggy; water every 3-7 days. Prefers cool temperatures (15-25°C) and struggles in heat above 35°C. Tolerates wide soil pH (6.0-8.0). Self-seeds freely — remove spent plants to control spread. Non-toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

four o clock.description: Old-fashioned garden plant with trumpet-shaped flowers that open in late afternoon and stay open through the night. Single plant can produce flowers of different colors simultaneously.
four o clock.care_tips: Water moderately — drought tolerant once established. Full sun to partial shade. Highly adaptable to most well-drained soils. Minimal fertilization needed. Self-sows readily — can become weedy in warm climates. Forms tuberous roots in frost-free areas and returns as a perennial; treated as annual elsewhere. Flowers in multiple colors (red, pink, yellow, white, striped) — often different colors on the same plant. Fragrant in the evening, attracting hawkmoths. All parts toxic, especially roots and seeds — toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

fuchsia.description: Graceful flowering plants with pendulous, lantern-shaped blooms in vivid combinations of pink, purple, red, and white. The quintessential hanging basket and shade garden plant.
fuchsia.care_tips: Keep soil consistently moist — fuchsias are heavy drinkers in warm weather. Partial shade essential; morning sun with afternoon shade is ideal. Direct sun scorches leaves and flowers. Rich, acidic, well-drained soil. Fertilize every 1-2 weeks during flowering with high-potassium fertilizer. Pinch growing tips to encourage bushiness. Hardy varieties (F. magellanica) survive to -10°C; tender hybrids are grown as annuals or overwintered indoors. Berries are edible (sweet). Non-toxic to pets.

gazania.description: Also known as: Treasure flower. Low, sun-loving South African daisy in the Asteraceae family with large, boldly striped flowers in orange, yellow, red, pink, and bronze that open in sun and close at night and on cloudy days.
gazania.care_tips: Water only when the soil is dry; it is very drought tolerant and rots in wet soil. Full sun; flowers stay shut in shade. Loves heat at 15-35°C; perennial in zones 9-11 and grown as an annual elsewhere, though it survives light frost. Low humidity preferred. Fertilize sparingly, once or twice a season at most. Sandy or gritty, sharply draining soil; ideal for coastal and gravel gardens. Space 20-30 cm apart; good in containers. Non-toxic to pets. Deadhead regularly to prolong flowering and cut back old clumps in spring; divide perennials every 2-3 years.

geraniums.description: Also known as: Zonal geranium. Popular annual and perennial flowering plants, include zonal geraniums (Pelargonium) and true geraniums (hardy geraniums).
geraniums.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist but well-drained (2-3 times per week). Allow to dry slightly between waterings. Full sun preferred for best flowering. Fertilize every 2 weeks with high-phosphorus fertilizer. Deadhead regularly to encourage continuous blooming. Pinch back when young to encourage bushiness. Research type (annual Pelargonium vs perennial Geranium) for exact requirements. Zonal geraniums (Pelargonium) are treated as annuals in most climates; hardy geraniums (Geranium) are cold-hardy perennials. Mildly toxic to pets—may cause GI upset.

globe amaranth.description: Also known as: Bachelor's button (not to be confused with Centaurea). Heat-loving annual producing round, clover-like flower heads in magenta, purple, white, pink, and red that hold their color when dried.
globe amaranth.care_tips: Water when the top inch of soil is dry; drought-tolerant once established. Full sun is essential — at least 6 hours for best performance. Average, well-drained soil is fine; thrives in heat and humidity where other annuals struggle. Minimal fertilizer needed; too much nitrogen produces foliage at the expense of flowers. Deadhead for continuous bloom or leave flowers for dried arrangements. Excellent heat tolerance makes it ideal for southern gardens. Non-toxic to pets.

impatiens.description: Also known as: Busy Lizzie. Shade-loving annual flowering plants in the Balsaminaceae family with colorful blooms, excellent for shady areas.
impatiens.care_tips: Keep soil consistently moist (2-3 times per week). Don't allow to dry out — wilting damages plants. Partial to full shade preferred; avoid hot afternoon sun. Bright indirect light is ideal. Fertilize every 2 weeks with balanced fertilizer. Deadhead regularly to encourage continuous blooming. Pinch back when young to encourage bushiness. Excellent for shady gardens and containers. Plant after last frost. Watch for downy mildew — choose resistant varieties if this is a problem in your area. Annual; grown for one season; no winter watering needed. Non-toxic to pets.

scientific_names: Delphinium ajacis (syn. Delphinium ajacis (syn. Consolida ajacis); Rocket larkspur)
D. consolida (syn. Consolida regalis; Forking larkspur)
larkspur.description: Cool-season annual with tall spikes of delphinium-like flowers in blue, purple, pink, or white, a cottage garden favorite and excellent cut flower.
larkspur.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist; does not tolerate drought. Full sun preferred in cool climates; afternoon shade in hot areas. Rich, well-drained soil. Fertilize at planting and again mid-season. Direct sow in fall or early spring—dislikes transplanting. Excellent cut flower. Prefers cool weather; declines in heat. Toxic to pets and humans (alkaloids similar to delphinium). Deadhead regularly to prolong blooming. Pinch growing tips early for bushier plants.

lisianthus.description: Also known as: Texas bluebell. Elegant annual or short-lived perennial producing ruffled, rose-like blooms in white, pink, purple, and bicolor; prized as a premium cut flower.
lisianthus.care_tips: Water at the base when the top inch of soil feels dry; keep soil evenly moist but never waterlogged, as lisianthus is prone to crown rot. Full sun to light afternoon shade is ideal. Neutral to slightly alkaline, well-drained soil produces the best results. Fertilize every 2 weeks during bloom with a phosphorus-rich fertilizer. Stake tall varieties to support the heavy blooms. Slow to start from seed (requires 12-16 weeks); transplants are recommended for home gardens. Non-toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

lobelia.description: Mounding or trailing plant with masses of small blue, white, or pink flowers; cools down in heat but rebounds in fall.
lobelia.care_tips: Keep soil consistently moist; avoid drying out. Partial shade in hot climates; full sun in cool regions. Fertilize every 2 weeks. Shear back midsummer if leggy for fall rebloom. Cool-season performer. Toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

madagascar periwinkle.description: Also known as: Annual vinca, Rosy periwinkle, Cape periwinkle. Heat-loving bedding plant in the Apocynaceae family with glossy leaves and five-petaled flowers in pink, white, red, or purple all summer; not the trailing Vinca minor groundcover.
madagascar periwinkle.care_tips: Water when the top inch of soil is dry; it tolerates drought better than soggy soil. Full sun. Thrives at 20-32°C and sulks below 15°C; plant out only after nights are warm. Medium humidity. Fertilize monthly with a balanced fertilizer. Plant in well-draining soil; wet, cool soil invites root and stem rot. Grown as an annual; perennial in zones 10-11. Self-cleaning, so no deadheading is needed. Toxic to pets; contains vinca alkaloids. Pinch young plants for bushiness; trim leggy stems in midsummer.

african marigold.description: Large, bold flowers in yellow or orange; pest-repellent and excellent for cutting.
african marigold.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun essential. Well-draining soil. Fertilize every 2-3 weeks. Deadhead to encourage blooms. Tall varieties may need staking. Repels pests. Mildly toxic to pets—may cause GI upset.

marigolds.description: Hardy annual flowering plants in the Asteraceae family with bright yellow, orange, or red flowers, excellent for pest control.
marigolds.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist (2-3 times per week). Allow to dry slightly between waterings. Full sun essential (6-8 hours daily). Fertilize monthly with balanced fertilizer. Deadhead regularly to encourage continuous blooming. Pinch back when young to encourage bushiness. Excellent companion plants - repel nematodes and some pests. Easy to grow from seed. Plant after last frost. Research variety type for size and bloom characteristics. Annual; grown for one season; no winter watering needed. Mildly toxic to pets—may cause GI upset.

nasturtium.description: Also known as: Garden nasturtium. Annual and perennial flowers in the Tropaeolaceae family with edible flowers and leaves, trailing or climbing habit.
nasturtium.care_tips: Water regularly but allow to dry between waterings (2-3 times per week). Prefer slightly dry conditions - too much water reduces flowering. Well-drained soil preferred. Full sun to partial shade. Fertilize sparingly - rich soil reduces blooms. Edible flowers and leaves with peppery flavor. Trailing or climbing habit. Attract beneficial insects. Annual; grown for one season; no winter watering needed. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

nicotiana.description: Also known as: Flowering tobacco, Jasmine tobacco. Ornamental relatives of tobacco in the Solanaceae family with sticky leaves and tubular, star-faced flowers in white, lime green, pink, and red; the tall species release a heady jasmine scent at dusk for moths.
nicotiana.care_tips: Keep the soil evenly moist; wilts in dry heat but recovers. Full sun to partial shade; the tall species prefer afternoon shade. Grows best at 15-30°C and is killed by frost; perennial only in zones 10-11. Medium humidity. Feed every 3-4 weeks with a balanced fertilizer. Rich, well-draining soil. Sow seed on the surface 8 weeks before the last frost; it needs light to germinate. Self-sows freely in mild climates. Tobacco hornworms and aphids may attack. Toxic to pets; all parts contain nicotine. Deadhead to extend bloom and stake the tallest species; cut back by half if plants flop in midsummer

ornamental kale.description: Also known as: Nagoya ornamental kale. Cool-season annual grown for its striking rosettes of ruffled or fringed leaves in purple, pink, white, and cream; color intensifies as temperatures drop below 55°F (13°C).
ornamental kale.care_tips: Water when the top inch of soil is dry; avoid overhead watering which can promote fungal diseases. Full sun (6+ hours) produces the most vivid coloration. Average, well-drained soil is fine; avoid over-fertilizing which promotes leggy green growth instead of colorful foliage. Plant in early fall for best display — colors develop only after sustained cool temperatures below 13°C. Technically edible but bred for looks, not flavor. Tolerates light frost and often looks best after a few cold snaps. Remove by spring when it bolts and becomes unsightly. Non-toxic to pets. Remove yellowed outer leave

pansy.description: Cold-tolerant flowers with face-like markings in many colors; plant in fall or early spring.
pansy.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist. Full sun in cool weather; partial shade when hot. Fertilize every 2 weeks. Deadhead to prolong bloom. Cool-season annual—plant in fall or early spring for best results.

pentas.description: Star-shaped flower clusters in red, pink, or white; butterfly magnet, heat-loving.
pentas.care_tips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun preferred. Fertilize every 2-3 weeks. Deadhead to encourage rebloom. Heat and humidity tolerant. Perennial in frost-free zones; grow as annual elsewhere.

grandiflora petunia.description: Large, trumpet-shaped flowers in many colors; showy but sensitive to rain and heat.
grandiflora petunia.care_tips: Water regularly; keep soil evenly moist. Full sun essential. Fertilize every 2 weeks with bloom fertilizer. Deadhead or shear back midsummer. Flowers may wilt in heavy rain.

petunias.description: Also known as: Garden petunia. Popular annual flowering plants in the Solanaceae family with trumpet-shaped flowers, excellent for containers and hanging baskets.
petunias.care_tips: Keep soil evenly moist (2-3 times per week). Water at base to avoid wetting flowers. Full sun essential (6-8 hours daily). Fertilize every 2 weeks with high-phosphorus fertilizer to encourage flowering. Deadhead regularly or shear back by one-third mid-season to encourage reblooming.
